#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Tweet length, media attached?
- Replies, retweets, quote-tweets?
- Search across all tweets in real time?
- Direct messages?
- Trending in scope?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Media attached | store media in object store plus CDN; the tweet row holds references only |
| Retweets and quote-tweets | store them as references to the original, not copies, to avoid duplication |
| Real-time search across all tweets | a near-real-time inverted index (Elasticsearch) fed by a tweet event stream |
| Celebrity fan-out | hybrid timeline: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities to bound write amplification |
| Direct messages | a separate chat subsystem with its own storage and delivery |
| Trending | streaming aggregation of hashtags/terms over sliding windows |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** post tweet, follow, home timeline, user profile, search, notifications, trending
- **NFR:** real-time-ish timelines (<5s freshness), 99.99% availability, handle celeb fan-out

**Scale**

- **DAU:** 500M (X-public 2024 order-of-magnitude; was 330M Twitter-2019). Assume 40% post on a given day, avg 1 post/day → ~200M tweets/day.
- **Tweets/s:** 200M / 86,400 = **~2.3k/s steady**. Spike multiplier ×20 for breaking news / sports finals (Super Bowl, World Cup, election) → **~50k/s peak**.
- **Read amplification:** users open the app ~5×/day, each session loads ~20 tweets → ~100 reads per posted tweet. 2.3k/s × 100 = **~250k/s steady reads**; ×20 spike → **~5M/s peak reads**.
- **Tweet record size:** tweet_id Snowflake (8B) + author_id (8B) + text (avg ~600B; ≤280 chars ≈ 280–840B UTF-8) + parent_id (8B) + media_ids[] (~32B) + created_at (8B) + entity refs (hashtags/mentions ~200B) + flags ≈ **~1KB metadata**.
- **Tweet write volume:** 200M × 1KB = **~200GB/day** metadata. RF=3 (Cassandra/Manhattan-style) → **~600GB/day on hot wide-column store**.
- **Retention:** indefinite for non-deleted tweets. 5-year cumulative = 200GB × 365 × 5 = ~365TB raw → RF=3 → **~1PB on hot tier**. Compact + cold-tier (>1yr) with ~3× columnar compression → ~70% storage saving on aged data.
- **Media:** ~25% of tweets carry media → 200M × 0.25 = **~50M media tweets/day**. Avg ~500KB post-transcode (mix of images ~200KB + short video ~2MB) → 50M × 500KB = **~25TB/day raw on object store**; CDN-fronted, hot 30d, then warm/cold tier.
- **Timeline cache/user:** home timeline capped at ~800 tweet-id refs (display + scrollback) × 8B Snowflake = **~6KB per user**. Cache hot 100M users (DAU subset that opens app daily): 100M × 6KB = **~600GB hot cache**; ×2 replication → ~1.2TB.
- **Search index:** every tweet indexed → 200M docs/day × ~1KB indexed payload (text + tokens + n-grams). Inverted-index overhead ~3× (postings + dictionary + skiplists) → ~3KB on disk per doc. 200M × 3KB = **~600GB/day**. Sharded Elasticsearch: hot=today, weekly rollups for prior 12 weeks, quarterly archives thereafter.
- **Trending state:** ~200 geo regions × top-K (K=1000 hashtags) × ~64B per (term + count + decay) = 200 × 1000 × 64B = **~13MB** live state per stream-processor task — trivial; fits in a Flink/Storm operator heap.
- **Celebrity fan-out:** top accounts have ~200M followers; on-write fan-out cost = 200M × 8B id = ~1.6GB write per tweet → use hybrid pull-on-read for celebs, push-on-write for normal users.

**Raw material, from the old Common Mistakes:**

- **Pure push fan-out.** A single celebrity tweet destroys the write path.
- **Blocking tweet ack on search or trending updates.** Those are secondary consumers, not part of the durable write path.
- **Storing full tweet objects in timeline caches.** IDs plus hydration is the right trade-off.
- **Exact counters on a viral row.** Engagement needs sharded or approximate write paths.
- **Global consistency for timeline freshness.** Users tolerate slight staleness; the system should exploit that.

**How to read the diagram:** this is mostly a feed distribution system. Tweets are stored durably, then copied or pulled into timelines depending on follower count, and finally enriched through ranking and cache layers before the user sees them.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** the social graph creates very uneven fan-out costs. Most users are cheap to distribute for, while a few are catastrophically expensive if treated the same way. The architecture reflects that asymmetry directly.

**What this layout buys you:** fast feeds for normal users and survivable behavior for celebrity traffic. The tradeoff is hybrid complexity: the system stops being one pure model and becomes a tuned mix of several.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Hybrid fan-out** (same as News Feed #8 — see for tradeoffs).

The threshold (~10k followers) is tuned per cluster load: below it, fan-out writes one tweet ID into N follower timelines on tweet creation, paying write cost once for read amortization across all followers. Above it, the tweet is flagged celebrity in the metadata store and skipped by fan-out; followers' read-time merge fetches the celebrity's recent tweets via a per-author cache. Concrete example: an account with 10M followers tweeting once would cost 10M cache writes (and 10M of cache memory across the cluster) under push; under pull, one cache write to the author's recent-tweets list and a fetch-on-read pattern that piggybacks on the existing read-side cache.

**Search index:**

The indexer consumes the tweet stream and writes to time-partitioned Elasticsearch indexes: `tweets-YYYY-MM-DD` for the hot index (today's tweets) with 1s refresh interval for near-real-time search, weekly indexes (`tweets-YYYY-WW`) for the prior 12 weeks, then quarterly archives. Tokenization extracts plain text, hashtags, mentions, and URLs as separate fields so queries can target each (`#bitcoin` is different from "bitcoin" in body text). Queries fan out to relevant time-window indexes only — "tweets from last hour" hits the hot index alone, "all-time tweets containing X" fans out to all live indexes and merges results. Ranking boosts recency (exponential decay on age) and popularity (engagement counts as a sub-linear boost) so the most-relevant tweets surface first.

**Trending:**

A stream processor (Flink) consumes the tweet event stream, extracts hashtags and key phrases per tweet, and increments a sliding-window count keyed by (region, hashtag). Each task maintains a top-K min-heap per region in local state — when a hashtag's count exceeds the heap's minimum, it replaces the bottom entry. Every 60s the heap is flushed to a per-region trending cache for client reads. Filters run inline: deduplication of near-identical tweets (Jaccard similarity over a content shingle) prevents copy-paste spam from inflating counts, and an entity-diversity check (unique posters, IP entropy, account age distribution) suppresses bot-driven trends. Time decay weights recent activity higher so a sudden rising hashtag beats a steady-but-old one.

**Replies / threads:**

A reply tweet stores `parent_id` pointing to the tweet it replies to; conversation reconstruction walks the parent chain. To load a thread, fetch the root tweet's ID then BFS forward through `replies` (a separate index keyed by `parent_id`), paginating per level. Deep threads (long Twitter "ratios") bound the BFS depth and load on demand. The reply graph is denormalized into a `parent_id → [child_ids]` index in the wide-column store for fast forward traversal; without it, finding all replies to a tweet would require scanning every tweet checking parent_id.

**Quote-tweet:** A quote-tweet is a tweet whose body contains the embedded reference (URL or `quoted_tweet_id` field) to another tweet. The hydration step on read fetches both the outer tweet (the quote) and the inner tweet (the original) from the metadata store, returning them together so the client renders the embedded card. If the original tweet is deleted, the hydration returns a tombstone the client renders as "this tweet is unavailable" — preserving the outer tweet's structural integrity without leaving deleted content visible.

**Direct messages.** DMs are out of scope of the public timeline path and run on a separate Chat-System-style infrastructure (#9): per-conversation message log keyed by `conversation_id`, with WebSocket fan-out for delivery to online recipients and a push-notification fallback for offline. Encryption-at-rest is mandatory; Twitter does not run end-to-end encrypted DMs by default (different threat model from Signal — server retains plaintext for spam/safety review and law-enforcement compliance). The DM service shares the user-identity and block-list services with the public-timeline product but has independent storage, scaling, and rate limits — a viral DM thread doesn't impact the timeline path and vice versa.

**Push fan-out vs pull-on-read for celebrity scenario.** *[Source: Twitter engineering blog, Manhattan papers]* The branching on follower count is the central economic decision of the entire system. Below threshold, push amortises N follower writes against millions of reads; above threshold, push catastrophically inflates write cost. The flowchart below captures the routing decision at write time and the corresponding read-time merge.

Concrete numbers: a normal account with 500 followers tweeting once costs 500 writes to follower timelines (cheap, fans out async, paid once). A celebrity with 100M followers under pure push would cost 100M writes per tweet — at 50k tweets/day from celebrities this is 5T cache writes/day, completely infeasible. Under hybrid, the celebrity's tweet costs 1 write to their own recent-tweets cache; each follower pays one extra read fetch to merge celeb tweets in. The break-even is exactly where total push cost (followers × write-cost) exceeds total pull cost (active-readers-per-tweet × read-cost), which sits around 10k followers given Twitter's 100:1 read:write ratio.

**Heron migration from Storm.** *[Source: blog.x.com/engineering — Open Sourcing Twitter Heron, InfoQ 2015]* Twitter's real-time streaming infrastructure ran Apache Storm for several years before migrating to Heron, an in-house replacement that maintained Storm's topology API but replaced the runtime. Reported gains: 6–14x throughput improvement, 5–10x latency reduction, ~3x reduction in hardware. The architectural change: Storm's thread-based worker model packed many spouts/bolts into JVM threads with shared queues, leading to back-pressure pathology and contention; Heron switched to a process-based model where each instance runs in its own JVM container with explicit metadata-managed back-pressure. For Twitter's trending and search-indexer pipelines, Heron's better tail-latency under bursts (breaking-news moments) made the difference between trending lag of seconds vs minutes. The lesson generalises: streaming systems with shared-process executors hit pathological tail latency under load; process isolation per operator is more operationally tractable at scale.

**Manhattan KV and Haplo (custom Redis).** *[Source: Twitter engineering — Manhattan distributed database, blog.x.com timeline architecture]* The tweet store is Manhattan, Twitter's in-house multi-tenant distributed key-value store with strong-consistency, eventual-consistency, and time-bounded read modes. Tweets are partitioned by author_id with per-tweet replication; the store provides durability and the cross-DC replication that the hot caches sit in front of. The timeline cache is *Haplo*, a fork of Redis with custom data structures — Hybrid List (a list-of-blocks-of-entries, optimised for append + range-scan) and a B-tree variant — added because plain Redis lists/ZSETs are not efficient for the specific access pattern (append-mostly, range-read with a moving window of bounded size). Haplo's hybrid list compacts older entries while keeping recent ones in fast-access blocks, so timeline append + recent-N-read are both O(1) amortised. The takeaway: at extreme scale, the right primitive may not exist in off-the-shelf tools and a fork is justified — but the fork inherits all the maintenance cost.

**Snowflake IDs as timeline sort keys.** *[Source: Twitter Snowflake — GitHub archive]* Tweet IDs are 64-bit Snowflake IDs: 41-bit ms-precision timestamp + 10-bit machine ID + 12-bit per-ms sequence. Crucially they're *roughly time-sortable* across the cluster (ms-level ordering is exact; intra-ms ordering depends on machine ID + sequence), so using `tweet_id` as the ZSET score in the timeline cache gives time ordering for free without a separate timestamp column. The 41-bit ms timestamp covers ~69 years from epoch; Twitter's epoch is 2010-11-04, so IDs run out around 2079. Clock skew between Snowflake-issuing machines bounds cross-machine ordering precision to NTP accuracy (~ms), which is fine for timeline ordering and not promised to be globally consistent at sub-ms precision.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Celebrity tweet** (Elon, 100M followers) — pure push fan-out would write 100M timeline entries per tweet, saturating cache write throughput and spending hundreds of GB of cache memory on one author's followers. *Mitigation:* mark accounts above a follower threshold (~10k) as celebrities; skip push entirely. On read, the timeline service does a separate per-celebrity-followee fetch (small, cached at the author level), merges into the push-built portion of the timeline, and ranks. The cost is one extra fetch per read, paid only by users following celebrities, and the celebrity author's "recent tweets" list is served from a single cache key shared across all their followers.
- **Trending spam** — coordinated bot networks can artificially boost a hashtag's count by mass-tweeting near-identical content, gaming the trending pipeline. *Mitigation:* score hashtag activity by entity diversity (unique posters, IP entropy, account-age distribution); a sudden spike from many low-reputation new accounts trips the diversity-low signal and the hashtag is suppressed unless organic users join. Time-decay weights recent activity but discounts pure-bot-cluster bursts; per-account reputation embeddings from a separate ML pipeline allow neighborhood-level dampening of known spam clusters.
- **Search ingestion lag** — when tweet write rate spikes (breaking news, sports finals), the search indexer falls behind and recent tweets aren't searchable for minutes; users searching for the trending event get stale results. *Mitigation:* the indexer applies backpressure with priority lanes — verified accounts and tweets matching active trending hashtags are indexed first, normal tweets queue. If lag exceeds threshold, drop low-value indexing tasks (e.g. tweets from accounts with zero engagement) and keep up on the ones that matter. Hot-index write amplification is managed by keeping it small (today's tweets only); rolling over daily limits the working set.
- **Hot tweet** (viral) — a single tweet getting millions of views generates millions of metadata reads, retweet-counter increments, and like-counter increments on one row, which the wide-column store cannot handle without sharding. *Mitigation:* CDN absorbs the media and the rendered card preview; the hydrated tweet payload is cached at the API tier with a short TTL (60s) so the metadata store sees one read per cache miss instead of millions. Counters (likes, retweets) are sharded across N keys per tweet — writes pick a random shard, reads sum across — so a viral cascade distributes load across many writers. Per-tweet DB rate limits prevent any single tweet from monopolizing the metadata store.
- **Mass-follow events** (new celebrity joins, 10M users follow within an hour) — naive handling writes 10M entries to the celebrity's followers list synchronously, saturating the wide-column store's write path on one row. *Mitigation:* the follow-creation API writes the per-user follow record (which is cheap, sharded by follower) immediately; the inverse index (celebrity → followers) is updated via an async batch process that smears the writes over minutes. Since the celebrity is above the push threshold anyway, their fan-out is pull-only, so the inverse index is mainly used for analytics and notifications, where minutes-of-staleness is acceptable.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fan-out | Async fan-out backlog delays tweet visibility for normal accounts | Publish-to-visible lag and queue-depth alerts | Keep tweet write ack separate, autoscale fan-out workers, and backpressure only the fan-out path |
| Timeline cache | Large timeline-cache shard loss causes rebuild storm | Cache miss spike and rebuild queue age | Rebuild lazily from author partitions and celebrity pull path, not via global backfill |
| Search indexing | Hot index falls behind during breaking news | Index lag and stale-search canary | Prioritize high-value or trending tweets and keep timeline writes decoupled from search |
| Trending pipeline | Bot spam poisons hashtag counts | Diversity-score anomaly and abuse suppression rate | Apply spam heuristics inline and suppress low-diversity bursts |
| Counter shards | Like/retweet shard totals diverge from event log | Counter-drift reconciliation metric | Reconcile against the source event stream and repair via explicit adjustments |
| Delete / moderation | Deleted tweets remain visible in caches or quote cards | Delete-propagation lag and tombstone-miss alerts | Hydration checks canonical tweet state, and quote cards resolve to tombstones when needed |

**Unresolved**

#### Answers to drill questions
1. Nothing fans out. The tweet is written to Cassandra and flagged celebrity; followers' home timelines do *not* get the push. On read, each follower's timeline service merges in the celebrity's recent tweets via pull. Avoids 100M write storm; pays small read cost per follower. *If pushed:* the threshold (10k? 100k?) is tunable per cluster load; can also be dynamic — fanout-friendly during low load, pull-only during peak.

2. Cache the unranked merged candidate set per user (push-built + pull-celebs). Ranking runs per request on top — cheap because the candidate pool is small (~hundreds). Switching ranking algorithms doesn't invalidate the cache. *If pushed:* if the ranker grows expensive, materialize ranked windows for active users and recompute hourly; lazy users get fresh ranking on demand.

3. Tweets stream through Kafka into Elasticsearch with near-real-time indexing (1s refresh interval on the hot index). Trade-off is hot-index write amplification — manage by keeping it small (today's tweets only) and rolling over daily. *If pushed:* if 1s is still too slow, fronted with an in-memory inverted index for the last N minutes that merges with ES results at query time.

4. Score hashtag activity by entity diversity (unique posters, unique IPs, account ages, content similarity). Bots trip the diversity-low signal. Apply time-decay so a sudden spike from a botnet is suppressed unless organic users join. *If pushed:* maintain a per-account reputation embedding; spam clusters share embedding neighborhoods, easy to dampen across the trending pipeline.

5. Fan-in side: writing to the celebrity's `follower_count` is one shard, easy. Fan-out side: don't add 10M entries to the celebrity's "followers" list synchronously; smear the writes over minutes via a queue. *If pushed:* if those new followers won't see the celebrity's tweets via push anyway (above threshold), the follower list is mainly for analytics — fully async is fine.

6. Snowflake IDs: 41-bit timestamp + machine ID + sequence. Sortable, monotonic per machine, no central coordinator. Use them as ZSET scores so timeline ranges are time-ordered for free. *If pushed:* clock skew between machines breaks strict ordering; bound it with NTP and accept ms-level fuzziness — Twitter doesn't need nanosecond global ordering.

7. Storm's shared-thread worker model caused pathological tail latency under burst loads — back-pressure propagation through shared queues was unpredictable, and a single slow bolt could stall a whole worker. Heron's process-per-instance model with explicit metadata-managed back-pressure isolated operators cleanly. Reported gains: 6–14x throughput, 5–10x latency reduction, 3x less hardware. *If pushed:* the migration was API-compatible (Storm topologies ran on Heron unchanged), which made it operationally feasible; the underlying lesson is that streaming runtimes with shared executors hit tail-latency walls that process isolation avoids.

8. Timeline access pattern is append-heavy with range-read of a moving window — vanilla Redis lists are O(N) for arbitrary access and ZSETs add per-write skip-list maintenance. Haplo's Hybrid List structure stores recent entries in fast in-memory blocks and compacts older entries into more compact archived blocks, optimising for the actual workload (recent appends + recent-N reads). *If pushed:* the lesson is that off-the-shelf primitives stop being optimal at extreme scale; you fork only when (a) the access pattern is stable and well-understood and (b) the team can absorb the long-term maintenance cost — both true at Twitter, neither true at most companies.

9. Tweet writes use strong consistency (you can't lose a published tweet); fan-out reads use eventual consistency (a follower seeing a tweet in their cache 200ms after publish is fine). Manhattan exposes per-request consistency so the same store serves both — strong for the durability hop, eventual for the high-volume read fan-in to fan-out service. *If pushed:* counters (likes, RTs) use eventual consistency with sharded counters (sum across shards on read) because the row-write throughput needed for strong consistency on viral counters doesn't exist.

#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **tweets** (wide-column store, partition by author):
  `(tweet_id Snowflake, author_id, text, media_ids, parent_id (for reply), created_at)`
- **follows** (wide-column store, two views): `(follower → followee)` and `(followee → follower)`
- **home_timeline** (sorted-set cache per user):
  `score=tweet_id (Snowflake = sortable)`, capped 800
- **search** (search index, sharded by time): tweet text + entities (hashtags, mentions)
- **trending** (in-memory cache): top-K topics per region, refreshed every minute

**API contract**

```
POST /tweet                body: { text, media_ids? } → { tweet_id }
POST /follow/{user}
GET  /timeline/home?cursor → [tweets]
GET  /timeline/user/{id}   → [tweets]
GET  /search?q=...         → [tweets]
GET  /trending?region      → [topics]
```

**Observability**

- **Tweet publish-to-home-timeline latency** — key freshness metric for ordinary accounts.
- **Home timeline p99 latency** — split into cache fetch, celeb pull, ranking, and hydration.
- **Fan-out queue lag** — the main write-side health signal.
- **Search freshness** — age of newest searchable tweet.
- **Trending update lag and suppression rate** — health and abuse-resistance of the trends surface.
- **Counter reconciliation drift** — protects engagement integrity on viral content.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** tweets and social graph replicate durably; home-timeline caches are region-local and disposable.
- **RTO:** fast for stateless read services; slower for cache warmup after a regional loss.
- **RPO:** near-zero for canonical tweet writes, relaxed for derived caches and indexes.
- **Failover cadence:** test cold-cache regional failover because that is the real user experience after DR.
- **Cross-region cost:** mostly media/CDN and tweet-store replication rather than timeline-cache replication.

### 27. Design Instagram
#### Problem
Photo/video sharing app with feed, stories, profile, search, DMs — at billion-user scale, with media as the dominant data type.

#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a photo lab that develops your picture into 4 different sizes and distributes copies to every pharmacy within 5 miles of your followers, so when they want to look at it, it's already there. The original negative sits safely in a vault. The product experience is "instant photo" but the reality is an assembly line running before anyone asks.

**The approaches people actually take:**
TODO. Two or three things a competent engineer might reach for, in plain language and before any product name, with what each one buys and roughly when it wins.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a user uploads a 4MB iPhone HEIC photo. The app requests a **pre-signed URL** from the API — a temporary web address that lets the phone upload directly to S3 without routing bytes through Instagram's application servers (which would make those servers a bandwidth bottleneck). The phone PUTs the file directly to S3. S3 emits an "object created" event to a queue. An **image processing worker** picks up the event, fetches the raw bytes, and re-encodes in parallel into four variants: 100×100 thumbnail (~10KB), 480px-wide small (~80KB), 1080px-wide medium (~300KB), and full resolution re-encoded (~2MB). Each variant is written back to S3 and gets a **CDN URL** — an address that routes through a content delivery network (a network of servers distributed globally that cache and serve files close to users). The post metadata (caption, location, variant URLs) is written to the database. The fan-out service copies the post ID into the timeline caches of the poster's followers. The app shows the user their post — using the thumbnail that was generated first while the larger variants finish.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Object storage (S3 or equivalent)** — a globally replicated file store that holds every raw upload and every processed variant. Near-unlimited capacity; designed for large binary files. You never serve images from a database.
- **Image processing workers** — a fleet of servers that re-encode photos into multiple sizes and formats. Workers autoscale based on queue depth. They also generate WebP and AVIF variants (modern compressed formats that are 30–50% smaller than JPEG at equivalent quality) for clients that support them.
- **CDN (Content Delivery Network)** — a global network of cache servers (hundreds of cities) that store copies of popular media. When a user in Tokyo requests a photo, they get it from the CDN node in Tokyo — not from a server in Virginia. CDN handles 95%+ of media requests, so the origin S3 server receives very little traffic.
- **Multi-tier CDN** — the CDN is organized in layers: city-level edge nodes closest to users, regional nodes that back-stop city misses, and origin (S3) as the last resort. Hot photos (viral posts) are pre-warmed to all regional nodes the moment the ranking system scores them as "rising" — so the first viewer in any city gets a CDN hit, not an origin fetch.
- **Sharded like counters** — when Cristiano Ronaldo posts a photo and receives 5 million likes in 10 minutes, that's ~8,333 writes per second to one row in the database. No standard database row can handle that. The fix: split the like count across 100 "shard" keys (`likes:{post_id}:{0..99}`). Each write picks a random shard. Reading the total requires summing all 100 shards — an extra step, but any shard only sees ~83 writes per second instead of 8,333.
- **Stories** — stored in a separate Cassandra collection with a native TTL (time-to-live) of 24 hours, so the database's own expiry mechanism deletes them without a background cleanup job. The object store has a matching lifecycle rule that deletes the media files 25 hours after creation.

**The thing that makes it hard — the upload spikes:** a global sporting event ends and 10 million fans simultaneously try to upload photos. The image processing queue has, say, 100 worker machines. The queue depth explodes — workers are processing as fast as they can but the queue keeps growing. Users see "uploading..." for minutes and abandon. The fix has two parts: (1) autoscale workers based on queue depth — spin up more machines within 30 seconds when the queue exceeds a threshold; (2) generate the smallest variant (thumbnail) synchronously in the upload edge before queuing the rest — so the user sees their post appear immediately in their grid even while the larger variants are still processing.

**Why this design and what it costs:** pre-encoding into multiple sizes at upload time rather than resizing at request time is the core efficiency decision. On-demand resizing means every viewer triggers a CPU-intensive resize operation on the server; pre-encoding means the resize happens once, and billions of viewers after that get the pre-built file from CDN with zero server compute. The storage overhead (4 variants instead of 1) is a fixed cost; the compute savings are proportional to the number of views. For a photo that gets 1 million views, pre-encoding wins by a factor of 999,999.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Upload: pre-signed S3 PUT URL → phone uploads directly → S3 event → SQS queue → image worker fleet (ECS containers autoscaling on queue depth).
- Image processing hot path:
  ```
  raw = s3.get(raw_key)
  decoded = decode_heic_or_jpeg(raw)
  variants = parallel_encode([100x100, 480w, 1080w, full], decoded)
  for each variant: s3.put(variant_key); cdn.prewarm(variant_url)
  db.update(post_id, status=ready, media_urls={...})
  fan_out_queue.publish(post_id)
  ```
- Counters: Redis with 100 shards per post for likes; a separate Kafka event stream for the audit-grade source of truth (exact counts from the event log, approximate counts from Redis for display).

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Media is dominant | an upload-transcode-CDN pipeline is the core; the feed stores references and multiple sizes |
| Stories (24h ephemeral) | a separate store with TTL expiry and a lightweight per-follower fan-out |
| Reels (short video) | a recommendation-driven feed and video transcode ladder, distinct from the photo feed |
| Direct messages | a separate chat service |
| Server-side image processing | a processing stage on upload generating thumbnails and filters |
| Billion-user scale | shard by user, cache hot feeds, and hybrid fan-out for high-follower accounts |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** post photo/video, follow, feed, profile, like/comment, stories, search
- **NFR:** fast image load (CDN), worldwide low latency, durable media

**Scale**

- **Userbase:** ~2B MAU (Meta-public 2024), DAU/MAU ~25% → **~500M DAU**.
- **Posts/day:** assume ~5% of DAU posts a feed item daily → 500M × 0.05 = ~25M; round up for multi-post users + Reels duplicating to feed → **~100M posts/day**. ÷86,400 ≈ **~1.2k posts/s avg**, ×5 spike → ~6k/s peak.
- **Stories/day:** stories use rate ~6% of DAU → 500M × 0.06 ≈ **~30M stories/day**.
- **Post metadata size:** post_id (8B) + user_id (8B) + caption (~300B avg of 2200-char limit) + media_url refs (~64B for 1–10 variants) + location (16B) + hashtags (~100B) + ts (8B) + envelope ≈ **~1KB**. Daily metadata = 100M × 1KB = **~100GB/day**; RF=3 → **~300GB/day** on wide-column store.
- **Media — original:** avg ~2MB/post (mix: photos ~500KB, carousel ~3MB, Reels ~5MB) → 100M × 2MB = **~200TB/day raw uploaded** on object store.
- **Media — variants:** server-side transcoded ladder: thumb 150² (~10KB) + small 320² (~80KB) + medium 720² (~300KB) + full 1080² (~2MB) ≈ **~2.4MB served set per post**. 100M × 2.4MB = **~240TB/day variants**.
- **Total media on object store:** raw + variants = 200 + 240 = **~440TB/day**. CDN-fronted, hot 90d (40TB × 90 ≈ 40PB hot), warm 1yr, then Glacier-class. Quarterly net add ≈ ~40PB raw + variants → **~PB-scale/quarter**.
- **Stories TTL storage:** 30M × ~1.5MB avg (short video ~3MB + photo ~500KB blend) = **~45TB/day ephemeral**. 24h TTL + 25h object-lifecycle grace → live footprint bounded to ~25h × 45TB/24h ≈ **~50TB hot**.
- **Likes/comments:** assume ~100 likes/post avg × 100M posts/day = 10B likes; comments rate ~5/post avg → 500M comments/day. Counter shard fan-out: 10B / 100 shards/post-key = 100M ops/shard-day → ~1k ops/s/shard (manageable). Counter materialized state ~100B per (post × shard) pair → 100M posts hot × 100 shards × 100B = ~1TB counter state.
- **Feed timeline cache:** 500M DAU × candidate set (~500 post_ids × 8B = 4KB) = 500M × 4KB = **~2TB hot**; ×2 replication → ~4TB.
- **Reads:** ~100× posts (every viewer sees each top post) → 100M posts × 100 = 10B feed renderings/day ÷86,400 ≈ **~120k feed-loads/s** steady, peaks ×5 → ~600k/s. CDN hit-ratio >95% on media → origin sees ~5% of 600k/s × ~2.4MB ≈ ~70Gbps origin egress.

**Raw material, from the old Common Mistakes:**

- **Resizing images on demand in the read path.** Precomputed variants are the whole point of the media pipeline.
- **Routing upload bytes through your API tier.** Direct-to-object-store upload keeps APIs from becoming bandwidth bottlenecks.
- **Treating stories as normal permanent posts.** Their lifecycle and storage semantics are different.
- **Exact counters on celebrity posts.** Hot content needs sharded or derived counters.
- **Serving full-resolution media everywhere.** Mobile feeds should bias toward appropriate variants.

**How to read the diagram:** the system combines a social feed architecture with a media pipeline. User posts first become durable media assets, then those assets and their metadata flow into feeds, stories, notifications, and discovery surfaces.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** serving images and videos efficiently is a different problem from deciding who should see them. Keeping media preparation separate from social distribution makes both easier to optimize.

**What this layout buys you:** scalable media delivery and flexible feed surfaces on top of the same underlying content. The tradeoff is that the content pipeline grows more complex as each new product surface reuses it differently.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Image processing pipeline:**

S3 emits an object-created event when the raw upload lands; the event triggers a worker (Lambda or a standing pool of containers) that fetches the bytes, decodes the source format (HEIC from iPhones, JPEG, PNG), and re-encodes into the four target variants in parallel: thumbnail (100×100, used in grid views), small (480px wide, used in feed cards), medium (1080px wide, full-view tap), and full (original resolution, download). Modern codecs (WebP, AVIF) are generated alongside JPEG fallback so clients with codec support get 30–50% smaller payloads. Workers autoscale on queue depth — an upload spike grows the worker pool transparently. Concrete example: a 4MB iPhone HEIC upload produces ~10KB thumb + 80KB small + 300KB medium + 2MB full (after re-encoding to JPEG/AVIF) within ~5s p95.

**Stories:**

Stories live in a separate Cassandra collection (`stories`) with native TTL of 24h on each row, so expired stories are garbage-collected by compaction without needing a sweeper job. Story media in the object store has an S3 lifecycle rule that deletes objects 25h after creation (1h grace beyond the row TTL). Highlights are an opt-in feature: when a user adds a story to a highlight, the underlying media is copied to a permanent collection (`highlights`) with no TTL, breaking the ephemeral lifecycle for that one item; the original story still expires normally. Viewer list is an append-only column on the story row — no indexing needed because it's only read by the story author looking at their own audience.

**Feed ranking:**

The hybrid push/pull fan-out from #8 produces a candidate set per user (recent posts from followees, plus pulled posts from celebrity followees). On read, a ranker scores candidates using signals: engagement prediction (will this user like/comment based on past behavior with this author and content type), friend affinity (closeness score derived from interaction history), time-of-day relevance (a workout post at 7am scores differently than at 10pm), and post-type diversity (penalize the 5th reel in a row to keep the feed varied). The ranker is a gradient-boosted-trees model or shallow neural net — lightweight enough to score ~500 candidates in <50ms. Ranking is per-request, so changing the ranking algorithm doesn't require invalidating the candidate cache.

**Discovery (Explore):**

Explore is a discovery surface for content from accounts the user doesn't follow. An offline batch job (hourly) computes per-user candidate sets via collaborative filtering — find users with similar interaction patterns and surface their recent high-engagement content. The candidate set is large (~1000 posts per user) and stored in a per-user cache. On request, an online ranker filters by content moderation flags, applies the user's block list, scores the survivors with a relevance model, and returns the top results. Refresh hourly is enough because Explore is browse-not-search; sub-hour freshness would cost orders of magnitude more compute without measurably improving engagement.

**Reels, DMs, filters, Live — scope.** *Reels* (short-form vertical video) reuse the TikTok-style transcoding pipeline (HLS/MP4 segmented variants, CDN delivery) and a separate ranker that's tuned for short-video engagement signals (watch-completion, replays); the storage and feed-merge logic share the post path so Reels appear inline in the main feed alongside photos. *Direct messages* run on a separate Chat-System-style infrastructure (#9) with WebSocket delivery and an offline-message queue per recipient — the DM product shares user identity, block lists, and notifications with the main app but has independent storage and scaling. *Image filters* (the colour-grade and beauty-mode effects applied at capture) run on-device in the client during composition — the server only ever receives the post-filter pixels, so the upload + variant pipeline is unchanged; the client embeds metadata about which filter was used purely for analytics and recreate-this-look features. *Live streaming* uses a dedicated ingest path (RTMP or WebRTC into a media server) → low-latency HLS for viewers, with viewer count and chat fan-out sitting on separate scaling domains; archived live videos are post-processed into normal video posts. All four are conceptually first-class but operationally separate codepaths from the photo-feed core; this design covers the photo-feed core in detail and treats the rest as bolt-ons that share identity, social graph, and CDN infrastructure.

**Upload → variant generation → publish — sequence.** *[Source: Instagram engineering / Meta CDN architecture]* The upload path is heavily decoupled: the API tier never sees the bytes, only the metadata. Variants are generated asynchronously off a notification queue, and the post is hidden from feeds until variants are ready. The synchronous-thumbnail option is a UX trick — the user sees their post immediately in their grid using the in-flight thumbnail while medium/full variants finish in the background.

Failure handling: if variant generation fails, the worker requeues with exponential backoff up to N attempts; persistent failure marks the post `processing_failed` and notifies the client. The metadata DB row remains as a tombstone so a retry can resume from the correct state without orphaning storage.

**Photo CDN architecture.** *[Source: Meta engineering / Akamai-style photo CDN]* Instagram uses a multi-tier CDN: edge POPs at user-proximity (city-level) cache hot variants for hours; regional caches (per-country/region) backstop edge misses and absorb invalidations; origin (S3 or Meta's f4 cold storage) serves rare cold reads. The CDN is keyed by full URL including the variant suffix, so `/photo/abc123_medium.jpg` and `/photo/abc123_full.jpg` are separate cache entries — invalidating one variant doesn't invalidate the others, which matters for variant-level lifecycle (full-resolution can tier to cold while thumbnails stay hot). For viral content, pre-warming pushes the medium and small variants to all regional caches as soon as the ranker scores the post into the rising bucket, so the moment users in any region see the post the bytes are already at their nearest edge.

**Cassandra → ScyllaDB migration (2024 patterns).** *[Source: ScyllaDB.com 2024 case studies — Discord, Expedia, Freshworks; not a confirmed Instagram migration]* Note: there is no public Instagram migration case study; the 2024 pattern is broadly applicable. Companies migrating Cassandra → ScyllaDB report 2–10x throughput on the same hardware and 10–95% P99 latency reduction (Discord: 40–125ms → 15ms read p99; Expedia: 80ms → 5ms p99 with 3x throughput, 35% cost reduction; Freshworks: 1s → 50ms p99). The architectural reasons: ScyllaDB is C++ with a shard-per-core thread-per-core model (no shared state, no GC), while Cassandra is JVM with a thread-pool model (shared heap, GC pauses). Migration patterns: dual-write via the ScyllaDB Migrator tool, validate row-level parity in shadow reads, cut over reads first then writes, retire the Cassandra cluster. Risks: ScyllaDB's stricter wire protocol surfaces previously-tolerated client bugs; CL=QUORUM behaviour differs subtly under failure; the migration's value is highest for read-heavy, latency-sensitive workloads (timelines, feeds) and lowest for batch-analytics workloads.

**Sharded counters — the precise math.** *[Source: Discord/Riot/standard pattern]* Splitting a like count across 100 shard keys (`likes:{post}:{0..99}`) means each write picks one shard uniformly at random, capping per-shard write rate at `total_rate / 100`. For a post receiving 50k likes/sec, each shard sees 500 writes/sec — well within a single Cassandra/ScyllaDB row's capacity. Reads sum 100 keys, paying 100x the read fan-out for the displayed count. This is acceptable because reads of the count happen on every post-render but each render only needs the count once; sharded read can be cached at the API tier with 60s TTL to amortise the fan-out. Exact-count operations (advertiser dashboards) read the underlying like-event log instead, which is the source of truth; sharded counters are a fast cache.
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hot post** (viral celebrity) — a Cristiano Ronaldo post pulls millions of metadata reads in minutes; the post's row in the wide-column store gets hammered, and feed services hydrating it overwhelm the metadata path. *Mitigation:* the CDN absorbs all media reads (origin sees one fetch per edge POP); the hydrated post payload (metadata + URLs + counter values) is cached at the API tier with a short TTL (60s) so the metadata DB sees one read per cache miss instead of millions. Read-replicas of the metadata DB scale read fan-out further, and per-post rate limits prevent any single post from monopolizing DB resources.
- **Storage explosion** — Instagram accumulates exabytes of media; serving everything from hot tier (S3 Standard) is prohibitively expensive when 95% of media is rarely accessed beyond the first month. *Mitigation:* lifecycle rules tier media by age and access pattern — hot tier (S3 Standard) for first 90 days, warm tier (Standard-IA) for the next 9 months, cold/glacial archive thereafter. Old media still serves from CDN edges if requested; cold-tier reads have higher latency (seconds for Glacier) but apply only to genuinely cold content. Variant-level tiering is possible: thumbnails stay hot indefinitely (used in profile grids) while full-resolution originals tier aggressively.
- **Image processing queue** — upload spikes (a global event drives 10x normal upload rate) cause the processing queue to grow; users see "uploading…" for minutes; new uploaders abandon. *Mitigation:* workers autoscale based on queue depth with a fast scale-up policy (add capacity within 30s); priority lanes route active-creator uploads ahead of brand-new accounts (which are also a spam vector); the smallest variant (thumbnail) can be generated synchronously on the upload edge so the user sees their post in their grid immediately while other variants fill in async.
- **Like/comment write storm on viral posts** — a Ronaldo post getting 5M likes in 10 minutes means 50k writes/sec to one row in the likes counter — single-row write throughput in any wide-column store caps in the low thousands. *Mitigation:* sharded counters split each post's like count across N keys (`likes:{post}:{0..99}`); writes pick a random shard, reads sum all 100 shards. 5M writes / 100 shards = 50k per shard total, easily absorbed; readers tolerate eventual consistency on the displayed count. For exact counts (advertiser dashboards, audit), a batch reconciliation job sums the like-event log — the log is the truth, the counters are a fast cache.
- **Mobile data usage** — serving the full-resolution variant to a mobile client on a 3G network wastes bandwidth, slows load times, and burns user data caps; bad UX for users in emerging markets. *Mitigation:* the API returns CDN URLs for *all* variants in the post payload; the client picks the appropriate one based on viewport size, device pixel density, and connection quality (Wi-Fi vs cellular, signal strength). Adaptive resolution: start with `small` and upgrade to `medium` if the user zooms or the post enters the viewport for >2s. AVIF/WebP variants are served when client headers indicate support, cutting bytes 30-50% over JPEG at equal quality.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Variant generation | Async media pipeline fails or stalls, leaving broken post assets | Upload-to-ready lag and variant-generation error rate | Retry at variant granularity, keep post in `processing`, and notify user only when required assets are ready |
| Story TTL | Story rows or media objects outlive 24h unexpectedly | Expired-story canary and TTL drift metrics | Use native row TTL plus object-store lifecycle rules, and copy to highlights explicitly instead of exempting originals |
| CDN invalidation | Wrong or stale variant remains cached after moderation/delete | Tombstone-hit mismatch and media-404 after delete | Short cache TTL for mutable surfaces and canonical tombstone checks before serving metadata |
| Counter shards | Like/comment shard skew or drift appears on viral posts | Shard-write imbalance and reconciliation drift | Increase shard count for hot posts and reconcile from append-only event logs |
| Explore / feed hydrate | Metadata DB slowdown makes media URLs unavailable even though bytes are hot on CDN | Hydration p99 and metadata-cache miss spike | Cache hydrated post cards briefly and serve partial fallbacks where possible |
| Moderation | Unsafe content becomes visible before checks finish | Time-to-moderation and block-after-publish metrics | Gate visibility on required trust-and-safety stages for risky uploads |

#### Drill questions
1. A Cristiano Ronaldo post gets 5M likes in 10 minutes — how does the counter survive?
2. Image processing pipeline backs up — uploads queue grows. What do you do?
3. How do you keep stories ephemeral at scale — TTL on billions of objects?
4. A user uploads CSAM / illegal content — how do you catch it before it's seen?
5. How do you handle 10x growth in upload volume?
6. A user blocks someone — how does that propagate to the feed and Explore?
7. Why are platforms migrating from Cassandra to ScyllaDB in 2024?
8. How does multi-tier CDN handle a post going viral globally?
9. How are sharded counters reconciled against the like-event log?

TODO. Only 9 drill questions carried over, top up to at least 10.
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Sharded counter: split the post's like count across N keys (`likes:{post}:{0..N-1}`); writes pick a random shard, reads sum all shards. 5M writes / 100 shards = 50k writes per shard, easily absorbed. *If pushed:* eventual consistency is fine here — users don't notice "1.2M" vs "1.199M". For exact counts (audit, ads), batch reconcile from the like-event log.

2. Autoscale workers off queue depth; if still backed up, prioritize: active uploaders' content first, brand new accounts last (anti-spam side effect). User sees "uploading…" state in app until variants are ready. *If pushed:* generate the smallest variant (thumbnail) synchronously on upload so the user sees their post in their grid immediately; other variants fill in async.

3. Store stories in Cassandra with native TTL; expired rows are garbage-collected by compaction. Media in S3 has lifecycle rule: delete after 25h (1h grace). No background sweeper to run. *If pushed:* "Highlights" copies the underlying media to a permanent collection on opt-in to break the TTL — a copy is the right model since stories and highlights have different access patterns.

4. Hash uploads against a fingerprint database (PhotoDNA-equivalent) inline with transcoding — block instantly on match. ML classifier scores other risk dimensions; high-risk content gets human-review hold before publishing. *If pushed:* high-velocity new accounts get a stricter policy (pre-publish review) until reputation builds; legal-mandated reporting for matched content.

5. Image processing is embarrassingly parallel — autoscale workers and S3 doesn't care. The bottleneck is metadata DB; pre-shard posts by user, hot tablets split independently. CDN scales independently. *If pushed:* the metadata write QPS is small per post, but read QPS for hot posts can spike — read replicas + cache (post hydrate cache by post_id, TTL 60s) absorbs it.

6. Block list per user, cached in feed service; merged into feed candidates as a filter at read time. Cheap because block lists are small. Search and Explore consult the same filter. *If pushed:* if blocks are huge (celebrities blocking thousands), use a Bloom filter for fast negative checks, full set for confirms; eventually consistent across services is fine — a blocked post slipping through for a few seconds isn't catastrophic.

7. ScyllaDB is C++ with a shard-per-core thread-per-core model — no GC, no shared state, no thread-pool contention. Cassandra is JVM-based with thread-pool execution and GC pauses. On the same hardware, ScyllaDB delivers 2–10x throughput; on read-heavy latency-sensitive workloads (Discord, Expedia, Freshworks) P99 latency drops 50–95%. *If pushed:* the migration tool (ScyllaDB Migrator) supports dual-write + shadow-read validation; main risks are that ScyllaDB's stricter protocol surfaces latent client bugs and CL=QUORUM behaviour differs subtly under failure modes — test extensively before cutting over writes.

8. When the ranker scores a post into the "rising" bucket, a pre-warm job pushes the medium and small variants to all regional caches in the user-proximity tier; edge POPs hydrate from regional caches on first request, so even the first viewer in any city sees a sub-100ms load. Origin only sees one fetch per regional cache, distributing load across ~50 regions instead of bombarding origin. *If pushed:* full-resolution variants stay at origin (rarely viewed, expensive to pre-warm); thumbnail and small variants pre-warm aggressively because they cover 95% of view bandwidth.

9. The like-event log is source of truth — every like is an append-only event in the wide-column store keyed by `(post_id, user_id, ts)` (also enforces idempotency: a duplicate like from the same user on the same post is a no-op insert). Sharded counters (`likes:{post}:{0..99}`) are a derived cache. A periodic reconciliation job (hourly per shard) sums the event log per post, compares to the sum of sharded counters, and corrects drift via an audit-trailed adjustment. Drift is normally zero because the counter increment is in the same transaction as the event insert; when it isn't (rare cross-region propagation issue), the event log wins. *If pushed:* for advertiser dashboards needing exact counts, query the event log directly via a materialised view that's batch-refreshed.

**Raw material, from the old Talking Points:**

- **Direct upload to object storage plus async variant generation** is the upload story.
- **CDN URLs only in feed payloads** is the read-story simplification.
- **Stories want native TTL semantics** rather than bespoke cleanup jobs.
- **Explore and feed ranking are separate recommendation surfaces.**
- **Sharded counters keep celebrity engagement bursts tractable.**
- **Media dominates the system, not text.** That is the architectural mindset shift for Instagram.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **posts** (wide-column store, partition by user): `(post_id, user_id, caption, media_urls{thumb,small,med,full}, location, ts)`
- **likes** (sharded counter store + wide-column log): per post
- **comments** (wide-column store): `(post_id, comment_id timeuuid, user_id, text)`
- **follows / feed** (same as Twitter)
- **stories** (wide-column store, TTL 24h): `(user_id, story_id, media_url, ts, viewers[])`
- **media** (object store + CDN), accessed via CDN URL signed if private

**API contract**

```
POST /upload                body: image bytes, caption, location, tags
GET  /feed?cursor           → [{post, author, likes, comments_preview}]
GET  /profile/{user}        → posts grid
POST /like/{post_id}
POST /comment/{post_id}     body: { text }
GET  /stories/feed          → ranked by recency × relevance
```

**Observability**

- **Upload-to-ready latency** — creator-facing asset pipeline SLO.
- **Variant-generation failure rate** — catches codec/regression issues early.
- **CDN hit ratio by variant** — especially thumbnail/small vs full-size variants.
- **Story expiry correctness** — fraction of stories still retrievable after TTL.
- **Counter drift against event log** — protects engagement correctness on hot content.
- **Feed media bytes per render** — critical mobile-performance and cost metric.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** media objects replicate broadly behind CDN; metadata is region-homed but globally readable via caches.
- **RTO:** media delivery survives most origin issues via CDN; metadata-region failover is slower but manageable.
- **RPO:** near-zero for post metadata and uploaded media after commit; story expiry is derived and can be recomputed.
- **Failover cadence:** asset-pipeline and metadata failovers both matter; pure API drills are insufficient.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by media replication and CDN egress, not by metadata rows.

### 28. Design TikTok (Short Video)
#### Problem
Endless personalized short-video feed with sub-second swipe-to-play, upload, and a strong recommendation algorithm.
#### Core
TODO

Write the whole answer as you would give it in sixty seconds, 200 to 300 words, standing alone.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a jukebox that watches you — every song it plays, it studies whether you fast-forwarded, replayed, or danced. The next song is chosen based on everything it has observed about you and everyone like you. But this jukebox serves 1 billion people simultaneously, and if the next song takes more than a fraction of a second to start, people switch to something else.

**The approaches people actually take:**
TODO. Two or three things a competent engineer might reach for, in plain language and before any product name, with what each one buys and roughly when it wins.

**The single-request walkthrough:** you open TikTok and swipe up. Your app sends your `user_id` plus context (time, location, device) to the Feed Service. The Feed Service retrieves your **user embedding** — a 256-dimensional vector (think of it as a point in 256-dimensional space that encodes your viewing history and preferences, pre-computed from all your past interactions). It then runs **ANN retrieval** (approximate nearest neighbor — an algorithm that finds the videos whose embeddings are mathematically closest to yours in that 256-dimensional space, from a pool of 10 billion videos, in under 10 milliseconds). Five retrieval channels run in parallel: the two-tower ANN result, trending videos in your region, recent uploads from creators you follow, diversity candidates (to avoid filter bubbles), and videos using sounds you have engaged with. These ~300 candidates go through a **ranker** — a small neural network that predicts your probability of watching each video to completion, liking it, and sharing it. The top 50 video IDs are returned to your app. Your app starts playing #1 and simultaneously downloads the first chunk of #2 and #3 in the background. When you swipe, #2 plays instantly from local storage.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Two-tower model** — a machine learning architecture with two halves: a "user tower" that encodes a user's history into a 256-dim vector, and a "video tower" that encodes a video's features into the same space. The critical property: the video tower runs offline (once per video, result stored), so at serve time only the cheap user-tower forward pass runs live. You look up your vector, then find nearby video vectors using an index.
- **ANN index (HNSW or IVF-PQ)** — **Approximate Nearest Neighbor** is an algorithm that finds the closest vectors to a query without checking all 10 billion of them. **HNSW** (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a graph where similar vectors are connected; searching it is like navigating a city by always moving toward the destination. **IVF-PQ** (Inverted File with Product Quantization) compresses each vector from 1KB down to ~16 bytes (accepting a small accuracy loss) and clusters them, so you only search the relevant cluster. At 10 billion videos, HNSW would require ~10TB of RAM (infeasible); IVF-PQ uses ~160GB.
- **Online learning** — interaction events (you watched 80% of a video, you skipped this one after 2 seconds, you liked that one) flow back as a stream. A continuous training process updates the **ranker** model every few minutes so a video going viral right now will be boosted in recommendations within minutes, not tomorrow. The retrieval embeddings update more slowly (hourly) to prevent feedback loops where the model's own recommendations distort its training.
- **CDN with HLS** — video is encoded into multiple quality levels (240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p) and chunked into 4-second segments. **HLS** (HTTP Live Streaming) is the protocol that tells the video player which chunks exist at which quality levels. The player downloads the next chunk before it needs it and adjusts quality based on network speed. The CDN (a global network of edge servers) stores these chunks close to viewers.
- **Client preload** — the app downloads the first segment of the next 2–3 videos while playing the current one, using background bandwidth. When you swipe, the video is already on your device and starts in under 100ms. Without preload, every swipe requires a network round-trip plus buffer time.

**The thing that makes it hard — feedback loops in online learning:** if the ranking model updates every few minutes based on what it just recommended, and users naturally watch whatever is recommended, the model's training data becomes a reflection of its own outputs. Imagine the ranker starts slightly over-weighting cat videos. It shows more cat videos. Users watch them (because cat videos are decent). The model sees lots of cat-video engagement. It shows even more. Within hours, everyone's feed is cat videos. This is called a **feedback loop**. The fix: update the retrieval embeddings (which determine what categories of content are even considered) slowly — once per hour from a longer historical window — as a stability anchor. The ranker (which scores videos within a fixed candidate set) can update fast without destabilizing the space of what gets considered.

**Why this design and what it costs:** the two-stage retrieval-then-ranking pipeline is necessary because ranking every video for every user is computationally impossible. Running the full ranking neural network on 10 billion videos per request at 1 million requests per second would require more compute than exists. Retrieval narrows 10 billion to ~300 in under 10ms using cheap vector math. Ranking scores 300 candidates in ~30ms using an expensive (but small) neural network. Two cheap operations compose to do what one expensive operation cannot.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- Retrieval: Milvus or Pinecone vector database holding 10B video embeddings as IVF-PQ; ANN query for top-1000 candidates in ~5ms. Five retrieval channels in parallel.
- Ranking: TensorFlow Serving or Triton Inference Server; MLP with cross-features scoring ~300 candidates; GPU inference cluster autoscaling on request rate.
- Hot path pseudocode:
  ```
  user_vec = embedding_store.get(user_id)  // pre-computed, 256 floats
  candidates = union(
      ann_index.search(user_vec, k=200),
      trending_cache.get(region, k=50),
      follows_feed.get(user_id, k=30),
      diversity_sampler.get(k=20)
  )
  scores = ranker.predict(user_vec, candidates)  // batch GPU inference
  top50 = sort_by_score(scores)[:50]
  return hydrate(top50)  // add CDN URLs, metadata
  ```
- Interaction events → Kafka → streaming consumer that generates (user_id, video_id, label) training pairs → online ranker update every 5 minutes.

#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Video duration limits? (15s–10m typically)
- Live in scope?
- Comments/likes/duets?
- Region-specific content (China vs global)?
- Cold-start (new users, no signal)?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Recommendation-driven feed | a candidate-generation plus ranking service is the heart, not a follow graph |
| Sub-second swipe-to-play | pre-fetch and pre-buffer the next few videos and serve segments from edge CDN |
| Short fixed durations | aggressive transcoding to small segments and heavy edge caching |
| Cold-start for new users | fall back to trending/popular content until enough interaction signal exists |
| Region-specific content | per-region content pools and compliance-aware routing |
| Comments, likes, duets | separate interaction services feeding engagement signals back to ranking |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** upload video, browse "For You" feed, like/comment/share, follow, search by sound/effect/hashtag
- **NFR:** sub-second video start, smooth scroll/preload, accurate recommendations, scale to 1B users

**Scale**

- **Userbase:** ~1.5B MAU (TikTok-public 2024 order-of-magnitude); assume DAU ~1B (heavy engagement vs other social apps).
- **Uploads/day:** ~5% of DAU posts → 1B × 0.05 = ~50M; round up for power-creators / Shorts cross-posting → **~100M videos/day**. Avg raw ~10MB (60s @ ~1.3Mbps source) → 100M × 10MB = **~1PB/day raw upload** on object store.
- **Transcoded variants:** ABR ladder = 240p / 480p / 720p / 1080p HLS segments + thumbnail (~50KB) + preview poster (~200KB). Re-encoding to multiple resolutions/codecs (H.264 + H.265) totals ≈ **~2.5× raw** retained. 100M × 25MB = **~2.5PB/day variants**.
- **Storage retention tiering:** hot 30d (recent + actively watched), warm 90d, cold long-tail. ~40% of uploads receive <100 views (long-tail) → tier to cold within 14d. Effective hot tier = ~30d × 1PB raw + ~30d × 2.5PB variants × ~60% hot-retained ≈ **~30PB hot**.
- **Metadata per video:** video_id (8B) + creator_id (8B) + duration (4B) + sound_id (8B) + hashtags[] (~200B) + manifest_url (64B) + thumbnail_url (64B) + moderation_flags (16B) + ts (8B) + envelope ≈ **~2KB**. Daily = 100M × 2KB = **~200GB/day** on wide-column store; RF=3 → ~600GB/day.
- **Interactions:** ~100B feed views/day (1B DAU × ~100 video impressions/day) × ~30 fine-grained events per session (impression / start / 25% / 50% / 75% / complete / like / skip / share / pause) → **~3T interaction events/day**. Each event ~150B (user_id 8B + video_id 8B + event_type 4B + watch_pct 4B + session_id 16B + context features ~100B + ts) → 3T × 150B = **~450TB/day on partitioned event log** (Kafka-tier). 7-day hot retention for online learners → 7 × 450TB ≈ ~3PB hot.
- **User embeddings:** 1B users × 256-dim float32 = 1B × 256 × 4B = 1B × 1KB = **~1TB user-embedding store**; hourly batch refresh.
- **Video embeddings:** eligible pool ~10B videos (full corpus ever uploaded; long-tail kept for retrieval). 10B × 256 × 4B = **~10TB video-embedding store**; ANN-indexed (HNSW/IVF) in vector store.
- **ML training feature lake:** 30d × 3T events × 150B = 90T × 150B = ~13PB raw; columnar Parquet+ZSTD ~5× → **~2.5PB on object store**.
- **Read traffic:** 100B feed views/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **~1.2M/s avg** → **~5M/s peak** (evenings/holidays). CDN hit-ratio >95% on segments; origin egress ≈ 5% × peak — handled by regional edges.

**Raw material, from the old Common Mistakes:**

- **One-stage ranking over the full corpus.** It is computationally impossible at TikTok scale.
- **No client preload.** Swipe-to-play latency is the product; without preload the UX breaks.
- **Nightly-only model updates.** Hour-scale trends are too important for that.
- **Using HNSW blindly for a 10B-video corpus.** Memory economics often force compressed ANN approaches like IVF-PQ.
- **Treating exact view counts as hot-path truth for viral videos.** Approximate or sharded counters are usually sufficient in the product path.

**How to read the diagram:** there are two loops running together. One loop uploads, processes, and serves video. The other loop observes watch behavior and feeds those signals into recommendation systems that decide what the next swipe should show.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** in TikTok, ranking quality is part of the playback experience. Serving bytes quickly is necessary but not sufficient; the platform also has to choose the next item well, again and again, at huge scale.

**What this layout buys you:** tight recommendation feedback and highly optimized playback. The tradeoff is that the recommendation loop becomes central infrastructure rather than an optional add-on.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Recommendation (the core):**
```
Two-stage pipeline:

Retrieval (millions → hundreds):
  - Two-tower model: user vector × video vector → cosine similarity
  - Trending in user's region
  - Follows: fresh content from followed creators
  - Diversification: not all from one creator/topic

Ranking (hundreds → ~50):
  - Multi-task neural net: predicts (watch_complete, like, share, comment, follow)
  - Combine into single score
  - Learn online from interaction stream
```

Retrieval uses a two-tower neural network: one tower encodes user features (interaction history, demographic, current session context) into a 256-dim embedding; the other encodes video features (creator, content tags, audio embedding, engagement priors) into the same space. Candidates are fetched by approximate-nearest-neighbor (HNSW or IVF-PQ) lookup against the video embedding store — the user vector becomes the query, top-K nearest videos are returned in milliseconds despite billions of candidates. Multiple retrieval channels run in parallel (collaborative-filter neighbors, trending-in-region, fresh-from-follows, diversity-injection) and their outputs are unioned. Ranking takes those ~hundreds of candidates and runs a multi-task model that predicts watch-completion %, like probability, share, comment, follow — these predictions are combined into a final score (typically a weighted sum tuned by A/B test). Top ~50 are returned to the client.

**Cold start:**

A brand new user has no interaction history, so the user-tower embedding is uninformative. Cold-start uses demographic-bucket defaults — age, region, language, device — keying into a pre-curated pool of "evergreen" content with high completion rates across most user segments. After the user's first ~10 interactions, the embedding has enough signal for normal two-tower retrieval to take over. A faster warm-start uses explicit onboarding (pick 3 interest topics) which seeds the user vector toward those topic clusters. For brand-new videos with no engagement history, the video-tower embedding is initialized from creator history + content features (CV embeddings of the visual track + audio embedding of the soundtrack) so they have plausible neighbors immediately rather than zero-vector cold start.

**Preloading:**

The For You feed response includes the first video plus prefetch hints for the next 2-3 videos. The client begins playing video #1 immediately and concurrently fetches the manifest + first segment for videos #2 and #3 in the background. By the time the user swipes, the next video's first chunk is already buffered locally — playback starts in <100ms instead of waiting for a fresh fetch. Preload adapts to bandwidth: on Wi-Fi, prefetch 1080p first segments aggressively; on slow cellular, prefetch only 480p and only one video ahead to conserve data. Preloaded-but-skipped videos are wasted bandwidth, so prefetch depth is tuned per network class.

**Sound / effects:**

A sound is a first-class entity (`sound_id` table) — every video carries a `sound_id` referring to either the original audio (the creator's recording) or a re-used sound from another video. The "use this sound" feature creates a new video that references an existing `sound_id`; the sound's `usage_count` increments. The sound page is just a query: `videos WHERE sound_id = ? ORDER BY engagement DESC` — surfacing all videos using that sound. This is the structural enabler of meme propagation: a sound becomes viral, every creator riffs on it, and the sound page becomes a discovery surface that compounds usage. Audio fingerprinting lets the upload pipeline detect re-used sounds even when the creator didn't explicitly select one.

**Live, comments/duets, China vs global — scope.** *Live streams* run on a separate ingest path (RTMP/WebRTC into a media server) with low-latency HLS or LL-DASH delivery to viewers; live videos appear in a dedicated Live tab and are eligible for the For-You feed only as recorded clips post-stream. The recommendation pipeline does not run on in-flight live streams (the candidate pool only contains finalised videos with embeddings). *Comments* are stored in a wide-column collection keyed by `video_id` with a separate sharded-counter for the visible comment count; comment ranking is a lightweight per-thread scorer (recency + author popularity + reply count). *Duets and stitches* are first-class derived videos that carry a `parent_video_id` reference; they're rendered as a side-by-side or stitched composite at upload time so the resulting file is a normal video that flows through the standard pipeline, while the parent reference enables "duets of this video" discovery and parent-creator notifications. *China (Douyin) vs global (TikTok)* run as fully separated infrastructures with independent content pools, recommendation models, moderation policies, and identity systems — they are not federated and a Douyin video does not appear on TikTok or vice versa; the design described here covers the global TikTok product. The architectural template is shared (two-stage recommender, online learning, CDN-fronted HLS) but the deployments, model weights, and operational teams are distinct.

**Two-stage retrieval + ranker pipeline.** *[Source: ByteDance / Pinterest / YouTube two-tower papers; Shaped.ai blog]* Every For-You request runs the same two-stage funnel: retrieval narrows ~10B eligible videos to a few hundred candidates via cheap embedding lookup; ranking scores those candidates with an expensive multi-task model and returns the top ~50. Multiple retrieval channels run in parallel and their unioned outputs feed the ranker; the channels exist precisely so the system isn't single-point-dependent on the two-tower model.
