**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| VOD only | pre-transcode an ABR ladder on ingest; no low-latency live pipeline |
| DRM required | a packaging/encryption step plus license servers (Widevine, PlayReady, FairPlay) |
| Offline downloads | issue downloadable encrypted renditions with an offline license lease |
| Multi-device profiles | per-profile watch state and recommendations, keyed under one account |
| Global low buffering | push content to edge CDN and ISP-embedded caches; origin only on miss |
| Personalized recommendations | an offline model plus a feature store serving per-profile ranked rows |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** browse catalog, play video, pause/resume, recommendations, search, profiles
- **NFR:** sub-second start, no rebuffering, global low latency, durable catalog

**Scale**

- **Subscribers / streaming hours:** ~280M global subscribers (Netflix 2024 public, rounded ~250M for older estimates); ~1B hours/week (public number) → 1B / 7 ≈ ~143M hours/day; assume 250M and double-counting downward → ~200M hours/day used here
- **Catalog size:** ~17k–20k titles (public estimates); each in ~10 ABR rungs × 4 codecs × ~5 audio = ~200 files per title → multi-PB (see footprint below)
- **Peak bandwidth share:** Netflix ~15% of global internet traffic per Sandvine reports; Sandvine global peak ~hundreds of Tbps → tens of Tbps for Netflix
- **Per-title encoded size:** 2 h × 60 min × ~10 MB/min at 1080p H.264 ≈ ~6 GB (rounded ~5 GB) per rung; 10 rungs × 4 codecs ≈ 40 video files; 1080p baseline (~5 GB) × half rungs lower bitrate avg → full ladder ≈ ~50–100 GB; pick midpoint ~75 GB
- **Catalog footprint:** 20k titles × 75 GB avg encoded ladder = 1.5M GB ≈ ~1.5 PB master library on origin object store
- **Open Connect cache footprint:** popular ~10% of catalog (~2k titles) × ~20 GB hot rungs only (drop AV1+top 4K) = 40 TB per appliance; large Storage Appliances ship with 100s of TB SSD, smaller Flash/PoP boxes ~20 TB
- **Per-stream bitrate:** 720p ≈ 3 Mbps, 1080p ≈ 6 Mbps, 4K HDR ≈ 15 Mbps; viewing mix weighted ~50% mobile/SD + ~40% 1080p + ~10% 4K → weighted avg ≈ ~4 Mbps
- **Aggregate bandwidth:** 200M hours/day / 24 h ≈ ~8M concurrent avg (peaks higher; Stranger Things drops hit 80M+ concurrent); 8M × 4 Mbps = ~32 Tbps; >95% absorbed by Open Connect inside ISP → AWS-paid transit egress sub-linear
- **Playback heartbeat volume:** 8M concurrent × 1 heartbeat / 30 s × ~200 B = 8M × 200 / 30 ≈ ~53 MB/s ≈ ~50 MB/s into Cassandra; 50 MB/s × 86,400 s ≈ ~4.3 TB/day raw

**Raw material, from the old Common Mistakes:**

- *Treating Netflix as "just a CDN problem".* The control/data plane split and Open Connect's ISP-co-located model are the actual economic story; without them the bytes don't pencil.
- *Letting bytes flow through the control plane.* Manifest+token+CDN-URLs from control plane; chunks always from OCA — coupling them ruins both economics and scalability.
- *Live-filling from origin as the default.* Live-fill is the bug; pre-position is the feature. Origin-fill rate must be a paged alert.
- *One ABR ladder for all titles.* Per-title content-aware encoding saves ~20% bytes at the same VMAF — material at Netflix scale.
- *Picking ABR rung at session start.* Network changes mid-stream (wifi contention, cellular handoff); per-chunk decisions are non-negotiable.
- *Synchronous DRM license issue per chunk.* Per-session token cache is essential; otherwise a viral launch melts the license server.

**How to read the diagram:** ingestion and playback are separate. Content is prepared offline into many encodings and chunks, then manifests and CDNs make playback mostly a data-delivery problem rather than an on-demand transcoding problem.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** viewers care about startup time and buffering, not about how elegant the encoding pipeline is. Doing the heavy media work in advance leaves the runtime path focused on choosing and delivering the right chunks quickly.

**What this layout buys you:** predictable playback and efficient global distribution. The tradeoff is large storage overhead for many variants and a substantial offline media-processing pipeline.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Open Connect CDN (the secret sauce):**
- Netflix-owned cache appliances installed inside ISPs (free for the ISP)
- Pre-positioned: predict popular content per region; push to edges during off-peak (3am)
- Reduces transit cost massively; most streams served from same ISP

**Encoding pipeline (offline).** Each title gets encoded into a per-title ABR ladder (typically 8–12 rungs from 240p to 4K HDR), four codecs (H.264 for compatibility, HEVC, AV1, VP9 for efficiency), audio per language (5.1 surround on supported titles), and subtitle tracks per language. The ladder is content-aware — animation has flat colour fields and benefits from a lower-bitrate top rung than live action with grain and motion. Encoding runs as a fleet of GPU jobs against the master file uploaded once; output is millions of small chunked files written to the origin object store, then later pre-positioned to OCAs.

**ABR (adaptive bitrate).** Client measures throughput per chunk and picks the next chunk's bitrate from the manifest accordingly. Modern players use buffer-based ABR (BBA): switch up only when the buffer is healthy (>20s ahead), switch down aggressively when it dips, because oscillation looks worse than a stable lower quality. Chunks are 4–10s — short enough to react to network changes, long enough to amortise the HTTP overhead. Per-chunk decisions (rather than per-session) is what handles wifi contention and cellular handoff smoothly.

**Recommendations.** Offline batch jobs train matrix factorisation and deep learning models on viewing history (watch %, completed, abandoned), producing per-user scores against the catalog. Output is precomputed rows ("Trending", "Because You Watched X", "New Releases", "Top 10 in Country") served from an in-memory cache keyed by `profile_id`. Even the artwork shown for each title is personalised — same title, different thumbnail per user, A/B tested heavily because thumbnail click-through is a measurable lift.

**Offline downloads.** Mobile clients can download a title for offline playback by fetching the encoded chunks from the same OCAs they'd stream from, plus a *long-lived* DRM license bound to the device that the player stores alongside the chunks. The license has a separate expiry (typically 30 days from download or 48h after first play, whichever comes first) and is non-renewable while offline — once it expires, the chunks are unplayable until the device reconnects and re-licenses. Region rights are baked into the license at issue time, so a downloaded title plays anywhere geographically until expiry, but a region-rights revocation invalidates re-licensing. Encoded ladder for downloads is restricted to the lower rungs (480p / 720p) to keep file sizes manageable; 4K downloads are usually disabled.

**DRM.** Widevine (Chrome/Android), FairPlay (Apple), PlayReady (Windows/Xbox) — three ecosystems, one encryption scheme (CENC) at the chunk level. License server issues a short-lived token bound to the device's DRM provisioning; without the token, the encrypted chunks are useless. Tokens are cacheable per-device for the session, so a viral launch doesn't melt the license server. Geo enforcement happens at token issuance — manifest endpoint serves a country-scoped manifest, license server gates on user's verified geo, so a leaked manifest still won't decrypt outside the licensed region.

**Viewing-session pipeline (manifest → chunk).**

The arrows show why control- and data-plane separation is the entire economic story: every byte the client sees as video flows from an OCA inside its ISP, never AWS. The control plane handles auth, manifest issuance, and the DRM token — small, infrequent, AWS-egress-acceptable. Telemetry is the only return path back into the control plane, and it's tiny (heartbeats every 30s, ~200 B). *[Source: Netflix Open Connect, Netflix tech blog]*

**Open Connect appliance hierarchy and fill sources.** OCAs ship in two general classes — large *Storage Appliances* (100s of TB SSD, hold ~all of the popular catalogue, deployed at major ISP cores) and smaller *Global* / *Flash* appliances (tens of TB, edge PoPs). Fill source priority for a chunk miss is: peer OCA on the same network → IXP fill from a peer OCA at an internet exchange → OCA at a Netflix backbone PoP → S3 origin (last resort). Origin-fill rate per OCA is a paged metric — a healthy OCA serves >95% from local cache and pulls fills from its peer set, never origin during peak. Settlement-free interconnect (free peering between Netflix and the ISP) is the deal that makes the program work for both sides; the ISP saves transit cost on its outbound peering, Netflix saves CDN egress. *[Source: openconnect.netflix.com]*

**Pre-positioning timing and popularity forecast.** Fill jobs run between 02:00-06:00 local time per appliance — the network's quiet window. A regional popularity model (per-country, per-region, per-show new-season-drop calendar) generates a ranked list of chunks each OCA should hold; the job pushes deltas, not full catalogue, so a single appliance only fetches the new-since-yesterday content overnight. Surprise hits trending mid-day can live-fill from origin or peer, but live-fill rate is alerted because uncontrolled it blows the egress budget. New-season global drops at Friday 00:00 UTC are pre-positioned hours earlier per region. *[Source: Netflix Open Connect distribution]*

**Per-title encode ladder optimisation.** A flat 10-rung ABR ladder (240p → 4K) wastes bits on simple content (animation, news) where the top rung looks identical at half the bitrate, and starves complex content (action, sports) where even the top rung shows compression artefacts. Per-title encoding analyses each title's complexity (motion vectors, scene cuts, grain) and picks a *content-aware* ladder — the same perceptual quality target hits different bitrates per title. Reported savings are ~20% bytes at the same VMAF (perceptual quality score) over the legacy fixed ladder. The cost is encoder fleet CPU — encoding a title now means analysis pass + encode pass × N rungs × M codecs (H.264, HEVC, AV1, VP9). *[Source: Netflix tech blog — per-title encoding]*
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hit show launch** (Stranger Things S5: 50M plays in the first hour) — if pre-positioning ran cleanly, each OCA serves its local ISP independently and there's no hot spot. The actual risk is OCAs that *missed* the prefetch falling back to origin/IX fill, which blows transit budget. Push to all OCAs in advance; multi-CDN (CloudFront, Akamai) as paid backup for OCAs that fail.
- **ISP congestion** (last-mile saturated) — Open Connect physically inside the ISP avoids the upstream transit link entirely; that's the mitigation. Without it, peak-hour video would compete with everything else over the ISP's transit and quality would collapse.
- **Buffering on slow networks** — clients drop to lower ABR rungs aggressively when buffer dips, and Netflix tunes per-network heuristics (cellular vs wifi vs fiber) so each environment picks the right starting bitrate. The cost is a brief quality dip, not a stall.
- **Region rights changes** (UK rights expire at midnight) — manifest endpoint must respect the new geo rules immediately. Catalog metadata service refreshes per-region views fast; the license server gates DRM token issuance on geo, so even cached manifests stop being playable.
- **Chaos / regional AWS outage** — control plane is in AWS, so a regional outage could kill new sessions even though Open Connect keeps streaming. Chaos Monkey forces engineers to test failover continuously; multiple regions stand active-active so a regional loss is a degraded mode, not an outage.
- **Origin-fill rate alarm** (an OCA falls back to S3 origin for a non-trivial share of chunks) — every origin fill pays AWS egress and breaks the no-transit economics. Healthy OCAs serve >95% from local cache and pull misses from peer/IXP fills; sustained origin-fill on one appliance is a paged alert pointing at either a missed prefetch or a popularity-model regression.
- **Per-title encode CPU** (encoder fleet runs analysis-pass + encode-pass × ~10 rungs × 4 codecs per title) — one title can cost thousands of GPU/CPU hours. Mitigation is amortisation: encode once, serve forever, and the ~20% bandwidth savings vs a fixed ladder pays back in days at Netflix's 32 Tbps peak.
- **Mantis / playback telemetry hot path** (8M concurrent × 1 heartbeat/30s = ~270k events/s) — the playback-quality feedback loop is what tunes ABR heuristics in production. Backpressure from Mantis must never block the player; heartbeats are fire-and-forget UDP-style with a small in-memory buffer per client and best-effort delivery.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open Connect | OCA dies inside major ISP | Per-OCA health probe + chunk-error rate from clients | Manifest lists multiple edges; player retries next-closest; cloud CDN (CloudFront) backstop |
| Origin fill | OCA falls back to S3 origin during peak | `origin_fill_rate` alarm | Pre-position better; peer/IXP fill priority; alert on sustained fill > 5% |
| Pre-position | Popularity model misses surprise hit | Live-fill rate spike | Live-fill from origin until next overnight push; capacity headroom in egress budget |
| License server | Widevine/FairPlay 5xx during launch | License-issue error rate | Per-device token caching for the session; horizontal scale; multi-region license servers |
| Control plane | AWS regional outage | Health-probe failures across services | Active-active multi-region; existing OCAs keep streaming for already-started sessions |
| ABR loop | TWCC misreads bandwidth (cellular handoff) | Client rebuffer rate | Per-network heuristics; conservative initial bitrate; aggressive switch-down |
| DRM enforcement | Region rights expire mid-stream | Manifest endpoint returns 403 | License server gates token issuance on geo; cached manifests stop being playable |
| Encoding pipeline | Per-title encoder fleet falls behind on launch slate | Encode backlog by `release_at` | Priority queue by ship date; codec/rung subset for delayed titles |

**Unresolved**

#### Answers to drill questions
1. Client manifest lists multiple edges; player retries the next-closest appliance, possibly one in a peer ISP or Netflix's IX presence. Brief quality drop while ABR adjusts. *If pushed:* if all nearby OCAs fail, fall back to AWS-hosted CloudFront — transit cost spikes but service stays up. Control-plane health checks reroute manifests within seconds.

2. Recommendation system already produces per-region popularity forecasts; combine with release calendar (new season ships globally Friday 00:00 UTC). Push to OCAs during 2-6am local. *If pushed:* for surprise hits trending mid-day, live-fill from origin to OCAs works but is expensive — alerting on origin-fill rate guards against runaway transit cost.

3. If pre-positioning ran cleanly, each OCA serves its local ISP independently — no global hot spot. Real risk is OCAs that missed the prefetch falling back to origin/IX fill, blowing transit budget. License server is a secondary bottleneck (every play needs a DRM token). *If pushed:* alert on origin-fill rate per OCA at launch; license servers are stateless and horizontally scaled, tokens cacheable per-device for the session.

4. Network conditions change mid-stream (wifi contention, cellular handoff). Picking once means buffering or wasted bandwidth. *If pushed:* clients use buffer-based ABR (BBA) — switch up only when buffer is healthy, switch down aggressively when it dips; throughput-based ABR oscillates.

5. Different pipeline: low-latency HLS/DASH (2-5s glass-to-glass) with origin packagers feeding edges in real-time, no pre-positioning possible. *If pushed:* live can't use Open Connect's cache-warming model; relies on conventional CDN topology (multi-tier edges, anycast); player tolerates higher rebuffer rate during peaks.

6. Catalog metadata service serves a per-country view; player requests a manifest scoped to user's geo (verified server-side, not client-trusted). At expiry, manifest endpoint returns 403 for that title in UK. *If pushed:* VPN evasion mitigated via IP reputation lists; the license server gates DRM token issuance based on geo, so a leaked manifest still won't decrypt.

**Raw material, from the old Talking Points:**

- **Open Connect is the entire economic story.** Netflix is ~15% of internet traffic — paying CDN egress for that is impossible. Lead with this.
- **Control/data plane separation** — lead with it, then explain the consequences (license server, manifest service, telemetry are all small-traffic, and bytes never traverse the cloud).
- **Pre-position over live-fill** — prediction-driven cache warming during ISP off-peak; live-fill is alerted because it breaks the no-transit economics.
- **Per-title ABR ladder** with content-aware encoding — animation gets a different ladder than action; ~20% bandwidth savings at the same perceived quality.
- **Per-chunk ABR via TWCC** with buffer-based heuristics — switch up only when buffer is healthy, switch down aggressively; don't oscillate.
- **DRM gates geo at token issuance** — cached manifests can't decrypt outside licensed regions, so leaks don't matter.
- **Chaos engineering as production hygiene** — Chaos Monkey/Gorilla/Kong continuously kill things so failover is exercised constantly, not just at game-day.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **titles** (wide-column store): `(title_id, title, year, genres, cast, ratings, ...)`
- **encodings** (object store + index): `(title_id, resolution, codec, bitrate, lang, drm_key) → manifest_url`
- **playback_history** (wide-column store): `(profile_id, title_id, position_sec, completed, ts)`
- **recommendations** (precomputed per user, in fast in-memory cache): `profile_id → [title_id, score]`

**API contract**

```
GET  /catalog?row=trending|continue|recommended  → titles
GET  /title/{id}      → metadata + manifest URLs
POST /play            → { manifest, license_token (DRM) }
POST /heartbeat       body: { title_id, position_sec, profile_id }
```

**Observability**

- `play_start_p99_ms` — target < 1,000 ms (manifest + first chunk).
- `rebuffer_ratio` — target < 0.5% of playback time; per-network breakdown for tuning.
- `origin_fill_rate_per_oca` — target < 5% during peak; > 10% pages.
- `oca_cache_hit_rate` — target > 95% inside ISP.
- `license_issue_p99_ms` — target < 200 ms.
- `pre_position_completion` — target 99%+ of predicted-popular bytes resident on each OCA by the regional morning rush.
- SLO: 99.95% playback start success globally; per-title VMAF (perceptual quality) target maintained across the ABR ladder.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** control plane active-active across multiple AWS regions; data plane (OCAs) is global by design — every appliance is independently servable. Catalog metadata + recommendations are eventually consistent across regions.
- **RTO:** ~30 s for control-plane regional failover (DNS / anycast); zero for already-streaming sessions (OCA continues serving).
- **RPO:** ~minutes for catalog metadata; zero for already-streamed bytes (the OCA cache is the canonical edge).
- **Failover cadence:** Chaos Monkey/Gorilla/Kong continuously kill instances/zones/regions in production; explicit DR exercises layer onto baseline chaos.
- **Cross-region cost:** dominated by origin → OCA pre-position bandwidth (rare per chunk, paid overnight); control-plane cross-region traffic is small.

### 32. Design Slack (Workplace Messaging)
#### Problem
Team messaging with channels, threads, DMs, search, presence, integrations — within isolated workspaces.

#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a building with many floors, where each floor is a company (a "workspace"). Within each floor there are rooms (channels). The PA system on each floor lets anyone in that room hear new messages instantly. But there's also a filing cabinet for every room — old messages go in chronologically, and there's a searchable index card system so you can find "that pricing email from March." The building manager insists each floor's records are stored separately and no one on floor 3 can accidentally reach into floor 7's filing cabinet.

**The approaches people actually take:**
TODO. Two or three things a competent engineer might reach for, in plain language and before any product name, with what each one buys and roughly when it wins.

**The single-request walkthrough:** a user on the Salesforce workspace types a message in #general and hits Send. Their client sends the message over a WebSocket — a persistent two-way connection (unlike a normal web request, it stays open so the server can push messages back instantly) — to the Message Server (MS Server) for the Salesforce workspace. The MS Server publishes the message once to a per-channel topic on the internal pub/sub bus. Every other MS Server that has at least one connected Salesforce user subscribed to #general receives the message from the bus and pushes it down those users' open WebSocket connections. Simultaneously, the Persist Service writes the message to a wide-column database (a type of database that stores rows keyed by channel and sorted by time — Cassandra is the canonical choice). The Search Indexer reads from that same persist stream and adds the message to Salesforce's dedicated Elasticsearch index. Total time from Send to delivery: under 200ms in the same region.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **MS Server (Message Server)** — a pool of long-running servers, each holding thousands of open WebSocket connections for users in one workspace. "Sticky" routing means reconnects land on the same pool so presence and channel lists stay warm in memory.
- **Per-channel pub/sub topics** — the bus that lets MS Servers talk to each other without a direct connection mesh. One MS Server publishes once per message; every other MS Server with a subscriber on that channel consumes once and pushes locally. This keeps fan-out cost proportional to how many MS Servers have subscribers, not how many users are in the channel — critical when a 100k-seat workspace's #general has 80k members who are mostly idle.
- **Persist Service + wide-column store** — durably writes every message to Cassandra, partitioned by channel_id and sorted by message timestamp. This is the source of truth, not the WebSocket path. If the bus crashes, messages are not lost.
- **Search indexer + per-workspace Elasticsearch index** — asynchronously reads the persist stream and indexes new messages within a few seconds. Each workspace gets its own index so a Salesforce query cannot accidentally return Shopify messages, and Elasticsearch's free-plan retention pruning can be applied per workspace without touching others.
- **Slack Connect bridge** — handles shared channels between two different companies. Rather than copying the message log into both workspaces (which caused ordering bugs), there is one "home shard" for the channel and all reads/writes from the visiting company route to it. The extra network hop on writes from the visiting side is the accepted cost.

**The thing that makes it hard:** imagine #general in a 100k-person company. A single message is sent. Naive delivery would mean writing to 100k recipients. The pub/sub design avoids that — but what about threads? A "reply to a message" naively requires scanning the entire channel partition for rows matching a `thread_parent_ts` column. On a busy channel this scans millions of rows for every thread view. The fix: a second Cassandra table, partitioned by `(channel_id, thread_parent_ts)` with message timestamp as the sort key. Loading a thread becomes a single partition range read — fast regardless of channel size.

**Why this design and what it costs:** the two-table pattern (channel timeline + thread index) is the canonical Cassandra pattern for this problem. You write every reply twice — once to each table — but that's a small cost: a write to two tables in one Cassandra cluster costs roughly the same as writing to one, whereas the alternative (scanning millions of rows per thread view) degrades linearly as the channel grows. Cassandra is chosen because it handles high write throughput gracefully by appending to sorted partitions, and it scales horizontally by adding nodes without resharding all data.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- One Cassandra cluster per workspace shard (or shared cluster with workspace-prefixed keyspaces for smaller customers). Two tables: `messages (channel_id, message_ts, ...)` and `thread_replies (channel_id, thread_parent_ts, message_ts, ...)`.
- Redis or a lightweight pub/sub service for the per-channel fan-out topics. Kafka sits in front of the persist path (Kafkagate pattern) so a viral message → 100k link unfurls does not OOM the worker queue.
- On every WebSocket message receive: publish to channel topic → await persist ack → return ack to sender. Never ack before persist.
  ```
  receive(msg):
    publish(topic=channel_id, msg)        # fan-out to online users
    cassandra.write(messages, thread_replies)
    elasticsearch.index_async(msg)
    return ack(msg.id)
  ```

#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Workspace isolation strict?
- Threading depth?
- File uploads?
- Integrations / bots / app marketplace?
- E2E encryption?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Strict workspace isolation | partition data per workspace (separate tenant boundary) for security and scaling |
| Threading | model messages with a parent thread ID and per-thread read state |
| File uploads | object store plus CDN with per-workspace access control |
| Integrations and bots | an events/webhooks API plus an app platform, adding an auth and rate-limit surface |
| Presence and typing | ephemeral pub/sub with heartbeats, not persisted |
| Search | a per-workspace inverted index updated on message write |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** channels (public/private), DMs, threads, mentions, file uploads, search, presence, integrations
- **NFR:** real-time delivery (<200ms), per-workspace data isolation, fast search, rich client (web/mobile/desktop)

**Scale**

- **DAU / workspaces:** ~30M+ DAU (Slack last-public 2019 + organic growth); ~500k+ workspaces (public); avg ~60 DAU/workspace; large workspaces (Salesforce-class) hit 10M+ msgs/day
- **Concurrent WS:** during business-hours overlap ~33% of DAU online → ~10M concurrent WebSocket connections globally
- **Message size:** ~500 B avg = (text ~200 B + msg_id/ts/user/channel ids ~80 B + reactions ~50 B + attachment refs ~50 B + JSON framing ~120 B); rich blocks (Block Kit) bump to ~2 KB
- **Daily message volume:** ~30M DAU × ~150 msgs/day/active user (Slack disclosed avg) ≈ ~4.5B–5B msgs/day × 500 B ≈ ~2.5 TB/day raw → Cassandra-class with RF 3 = ~7.5 TB/day stored
- **Annual message storage:** 2.5 TB/day × 365 ≈ ~900 TB/yr raw; free-plan 90-day retention trims ~40% of historical ingest → ~550 TB/yr effective hot
- **File uploads:** ~30M DAU × ~1.5 files/user/day ≈ ~50M files/day; 500 KB avg (mix of pasted images, docs, screenshots) → 50M × 500 KB ≈ ~25 TB/day on object store
- **Search-index per large workspace:** 10M msgs/day × 5 yr × 500 B ≈ 10M × 1825 × 500 B ≈ ~9 TB indexed; tier-1 enterprise customers get dedicated ES clusters for query isolation
- **WebSocket fan-out:** 10M concurrent users × ~5 channels avg active subscription = 50M topic subscriptions; per-channel pub/sub fan-out keeps each msg cost at O(MS-servers-with-subscribers) ≪ O(workspace_users)
- **Mention/notification stream:** ~5% of messages mention someone (industry heuristic) → 5B × 5% = ~250M mentions/day → 250M / 86,400 ≈ ~2.9k/s avg; 10× business-hours peak → ~30k/s on Notif dispatcher

**Raw material, from the old Common Mistakes:**

- *Treating Slack like generic chat.* Per-workspace sharding is the foundation of the design — without it, every operation becomes a cross-tenant query and compliance/retention/isolation become nightmares.
- *Replicating cross-workspace messages for Slack Connect.* Slack tried it and abandoned it because dual logs produced unfixable ordering bugs; single-home + bridge is the correct pattern. The cross-shard hop on visitor writes is the price.
- *Putting the WebSocket path on the critical write path.* WS is additive; persist (Cassandra + Notif) is canonical. A deploy that severs WS connections must not lose data.
- *Naive thread loading from the channel partition.* Filtering a channel partition by `thread_parent_ts` scans everything — denormalised second table partitioned by `(channel_id, thread_parent_ts)` is the canonical Cassandra fix.
- *Globally scoped search index.* Per-workspace indices are a hard requirement: ACL isolation, perf isolation, plan-tier retention.
- *Synchronous bot/integration fan-out.* A runaway bot can DoS the bus; per-app rate limits at the API tier are non-negotiable.

**How to read the diagram:** the architecture has a live side and a history side. WebSocket connections make channels and DMs feel instant, while durable storage and indexing make those same messages searchable and recoverable later.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** enterprise messaging is not just about delivery. Teams expect presence, threads, history, permissions, and search to work together. That pushes the design beyond a simple chat server.

**What this layout buys you:** responsive collaboration plus long-term retrieval. The tradeoff is that tenancy and search become core architectural concerns instead of optional features.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**Real-time delivery.** Each client opens one WebSocket to its workspace's MS Server pool, sticky-routed by workspace ID so reconnects land on the same pool (warm presence + cached channel list). Posting is fanned via per-channel pub/sub: the originating MS Server publishes once to `topic:{channel_id}`, and every other MS Server in the workspace that has at least one subscribed client consumes once and pushes to those clients locally. This keeps fan-out cost at O(MS-servers-with-subscribers), not O(channel-members) and not O(workspace-clients) — a critical scaling property for a 100k-seat workspace where most users aren't in any given channel.

**Threads.** A reply is a normal message with `thread_parent_ts` set to the parent's `message_ts`. *Threading is single-level by design* — a "reply to a reply" still attaches to the same `thread_parent_ts`, so the conversation flattens to parent + ordered replies (no recursive tree). This is a product choice to avoid Reddit-style nesting, and it keeps the data model trivial: one column, not a materialised path. The trick is read patterns: loading a thread is "give me all messages with `thread_parent_ts = X`" — naive, this scans the entire channel partition. The fix is a denormalised second table partitioned by `(channel_id, thread_parent_ts)` with `message_ts` as the clustering key, written alongside the main `messages` table; loading a thread is then one partition range read. Thread participants (anyone who replied or was mentioned) get pushed updates via a thread-specific pub/sub topic, distinct from the parent channel's topic, so a noisy thread doesn't pollute every channel member.

**E2E encryption (Enterprise Key Management).** Slack does *not* offer strict end-to-end encryption — server-side search, link unfurls, integrations, and DLP all need plaintext. Instead, paying enterprise customers get *Enterprise Key Management* (EKM): each workspace's messages and files are encrypted at rest with a customer-controlled key in their own AWS KMS, and the customer can revoke the key to make their workspace unreadable on demand. Trade-off is explicit: no E2E (Slack still decrypts server-side for indexing), but the customer holds the off-switch. True E2E would break server-side search and the bot ecosystem — a product trade-off Slack consciously declined.

**Notifications.** Mentions (`@user`) pierce do-not-disturb because they're high-signal; DMs always notify; channel messages respect per-channel-per-user preferences (all / mentions only / nothing). Notif Service consumes the persist stream (not the WebSocket fan-out path), so notifications are delivered regardless of whether the user is online — APNs/FCM is the path of record. Dedupe via `(user_id, message_ts)` so a reconnect doesn't double-notify.

**Search.** Each workspace has its own dedicated ES index, sized by message volume. New messages index asynchronously off the persist stream — search is eventually consistent (a few seconds lag), which is fine because the user just posted it and can see it in their channel. Filters (`from:user`, `in:channel`, `before:date`) compile to ES query DSL on indexed fields. Per-workspace indices give natural ACL (no cross-tenant leak risk in query construction), perf isolation (one big workspace can't slow another's search), and per-plan retention (free-tier indices auto-prune past 90 days).

**Integrations / bots.** Incoming webhooks let external systems POST a payload to a per-workspace URL; outgoing webhooks fire to external services on matching events. The App framework runs apps against an OAuth-scoped token; Slack hosts a limited bot-server fleet and forwards channel events to the app's webhook endpoint. Per-app rate limits at the API gateway protect the workspace's bus — a runaway bot can't fan-out faster than its bucket allows.

**Slack Connect (cross-workspace shared channels).** Slack abandoned the obvious "replicate the channel into both shards" model — it caused inconsistent message ordering across the two copies and double-write integrity bugs. Instead, a shared channel has *one* authoritative shard (the channel's *home* workspace), and reads/writes from the other side route to that home shard. A `shared_channels` bridge table on each participating workspace stores `(channel_id, home_shard, local_overrides)` — each side can override the channel name and topic locally, but the message log is single-source. Cross-workspace user identity required extending the edge cache (Flannel) to expose external user objects only when the viewer shares a channel with that user, so the identity boundary is per-channel rather than per-workspace. *[Source: Slack engineering — How Slack built shared channels]*

The expensive part is the cross-shard hop on writes from the *visiting* workspace — a User B reaction crosses Shard Y → Home Shard X. Slack accepts this latency because the alternative (replicating the message log on both shards) creates ordering bugs that are unfixable without a global consensus on every message. The bridge layer carries channel events, not user state; user identity is resolved on-demand via Flannel scoped per-channel-membership. *[Source: Slack engineering]*

**Job queue: Kafka + Redis (post-2016 architecture).** Slack runs ~1.4 B background jobs/day at 33k peak — push notifications, link unfurls, calendar reminders, billing — all fed off the persist stream. The original Redis-only queue had two bugs: client app servers held N×M connections (every client to every Redis), and adding workers raised polling pressure on already-stressed Redis. The fix layered Kafka in front: PHP/Hack web servers POST jobs to *Kafkagate* (Go), which writes them to a 32-partition Kafka topic with replication factor 3 and 2-day retention. *JQRelay* (Go) pulls from Kafka and pushes to the Redis worker queues; Consul-based locks let JQRelay self-elect per partition. Result: enqueue rate decoupled from execute capacity, durable storage instead of lossy in-memory, and Redis stops being a single point of memory pressure. *[Source: Slack engineering — scaling Slack's job queue]*
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Hot channel** (#general at 10am, 100k members all online) — naive per-recipient delivery would be O(members) writes per message. Per-channel pub/sub topic flips this to O(MS-servers-with-subscribers) — each MS Server consumes the message once and locally pushes to its connected subscribers. Cost stays bounded regardless of how many members the channel has.
- **Workspace shard hot** (Salesforce-sized customer: 100k seats, 10M msgs/day) — the workspace's single shard saturates DB writes, ES index size, and MS Server pool capacity. Split that one workspace across multiple sub-shards keyed by channel range; cross-shard mention search for that workspace becomes a fan-out query, but everyone else is unaffected.
- **Message edit/delete** — original message is already cached on every viewer's client and indexed in ES. Edits/deletes propagate as separate events on the same channel topic; clients reconcile by `message_ts` (replace local copy), and the search index updates via the same persist stream.
- **Search cardinality per workspace** — a 5-year history at 10M msgs/day is multi-TB per ES index. Per-workspace sizing keeps any one index manageable; free-plan retention caps (90 days) trim ~40% of ingest at index time. Tier-1 enterprise customers run on dedicated search clusters so their query patterns don't contend with anyone else's.
- **WebSocket connection storm on deploy** (10M concurrent connections all reconnecting at once) — without jitter, the surviving servers melt. Drain-mode deploys move connections off N% of the pool at a time, never all at once; clients use exponential backoff + jitter on reconnect; new servers do token-bucket admission so they don't accept faster than their warmup allows. Replay-from-cursor (last-seen `message_ts`) on reconnect avoids refetching entire history.
- **Slack Connect cross-shard hop on visitor writes** — User B reacting from a non-home shard pays an extra hop to write into the channel's home shard. Mitigation is acceptance: replicating the log to avoid the hop reintroduces the ordering bugs that drove Slack away from replication in the first place. Latency budget for cross-workspace reactions is generous (<1s acceptable) because the home-shard hop is amortised across many users.
- **Job queue Redis memory pressure** (pre-Kafka architecture) — Redis was both queue and durability, so a sudden burst (a viral message triggering 100k unfurls) could OOM the cluster. Mitigation was the Kafka-in-front pattern: jobs land durably in Kafka with 2-day retention, JQRelay paces them into Redis at consumption rate. Enqueue spike no longer threatens the worker tier. *[Source: Slack engineering job queue]*
- **Flannel identity cache cardinality on Slack Connect** — per-channel ACL means an external user becomes visible to many workspaces simultaneously; Flannel must hold profile + presence for the union of viewers across all shared channels. Mitigation is per-channel scoping (only resolve external users when the viewer is co-membered) and aggressive TTL on cached external profiles.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| MS Server pool | Deploy kills a workspace's WS pool simultaneously | Reconnect storm metric on surviving servers | Drain-mode rollouts (N% at a time); jittered exponential backoff on client; token-bucket admission on new servers |
| Pub/Sub bus | Per-channel topic stalled (consumer lag) | Topic lag alarm | Replay-from-cursor on reconnect against Cassandra; bus is additive, not authoritative |
| Persist Service | Cassandra write timeout | Per-keyspace 5xx + latency p99 | Async retries with idempotent message_ts (ULID); pubsub publish only on persist ack |
| Search index | ES indexer lag on a hot workspace | Per-workspace index lag | Per-workspace clusters for tier-1 enterprise; fan-out indexer with backpressure |
| Workspace shard | Salesforce-class workspace saturates its shard | Per-shard CPU + IO + ES heap | Split that workspace across sub-shards keyed by channel range; cross-shard search becomes fan-out for that workspace only |
| Slack Connect bridge | Home shard outage breaks shared channel reads/writes | Cross-shard hop error rate | Read-path fallback to bridge's last cached state; writes 5xx with retry; never replicate the log |
| Job queue | Redis worker queue OOM under viral message | Redis memory + queue depth | Kafka-in-front (Kafkagate + JQRelay) buffers durably with 2-day retention; Redis is execute-not-store |
| Notif fan-out | APNs/FCM 5xx during mention storm | Push provider error rate | Per-provider retry queue; dedupe via `(user_id, message_ts)`; graceful degradation to in-app badge |

**Unresolved**

#### Drill questions
1. Half a workspace's WebSocket pool gets killed by a deploy. What happens?
2. A workspace grows from 1k to 100k seats overnight (Salesforce buys a startup). What breaks?
3. How do you ensure mention notifications aren't lost if the user is offline?
4. How does threading not destroy Cassandra partitions?
5. A bot in a popular workspace posts 1000 messages/minute. Defenses?
6. How is data isolation enforced between workspaces in shared infrastructure?

TODO. Only 6 drill questions carried over, top up to at least 10.
#### Answers to drill questions
1. Clients see disconnect, reconnect with exponential backoff + jitter to a healthy MS server. Drain-mode deploys move connections off N% of pool at a time, never all at once. *If pushed:* without jitter you get a thundering herd reconnect; mitigate with token-bucket admission on new servers and replay-from-cursor (last-seen ts) so clients don't refetch entire history.

2. That workspace's shard saturates — DB write throughput, ES index size, MS server pool all grow linearly with members and message volume. *If pushed:* split the workspace across multiple shards keyed by channel range; introduces cross-shard mention search but it's tractable. Or vertically scale the shard hardware as a stopgap.

3. Persist Service writes the message to Cassandra, then publishes; Notif Service consumes the same stream and delivers via APNs/FCM regardless of online state. WebSocket path is additive, not authoritative. *If pushed:* deduplicate via `(user_id, message_ts)` so reconnect doesn't double-notify; mobile push has platform-side retry on failure.

4. Maintain a second table partitioned by `(channel_id, thread_parent_ts)` with `message_ts` as the clustering key — loading a thread is then a single-partition range read, not a filter on the whole channel partition. The main `messages` table stays partitioned by `channel_id` for the channel timeline. *If pushed:* writes go to both tables (denormalized); very long threads (1000+ replies) still fit in one partition fine; secondary indexes on the channel partition would work but degrade under write load — denormalized table is the canonical Cassandra fix.

5. Per-bot rate limits at the API layer (token bucket per workspace+app); workspace admins can throttle or revoke OAuth scopes. *If pushed:* fan-out cost capped via pub/sub decoupling; backpressure on the bot's webhook with 429s; alerting on per-app message volume anomalies.

6. Every query is scoped by `workspace_id` at the application layer; cross-workspace queries forbidden by code review and integration tests. ES indices are physically separate per workspace. *If pushed:* compliance customers (healthcare, gov) get dedicated shards; encryption keys are per-workspace via KMS, so even at storage one workspace's data is unreadable to another's keys.

**Raw material, from the old Talking Points:**

- **Per-workspace sharding** is the organising principle — say it first. Every operation is single-shard until Slack Connect explicitly crosses the boundary.
- **WebSocket is additive, persist is canonical** — message integrity comes from Cassandra + Notif, not from the bus.
- **Slack Connect uses single-home + bridge, not replication** — Slack abandoned replication because dual logs produced unfixable ordering; the cross-shard hop on visitor writes is the accepted cost.
- **Per-channel pub/sub topics** keep fan-out at O(MS-servers-with-subscribers), not O(channel-members).
- **Threads via denormalised second table** partitioned by `(channel_id, thread_parent_ts)` — naive secondary-index queries scan whole channel partitions.
- **Drain-mode deploys + jittered backoff** for the WS reconnect storm — without this, deploys melt the surviving pool.
- **Kafkagate + JQRelay** in front of Redis for the job queue — durable buffering for viral message → 100k unfurls without OOMing the worker tier.
#### Appendix
**Data model**

- **workspaces** (transactional meta store): `(ws_id, name, plan, primary_shard)`
- **channels** (wide-column store per-workspace): `(channel_id, type, members[], created_at)`
- **messages** (wide-column store, partition by channel_id):
  `(channel_id, message_ts (ulid), user_id, text, thread_parent_ts?, edits, reactions)`
- **search index** (per workspace): all messages tokenized
- **files** (object store + signed URLs per workspace)

**API contract**

```
WebSocket (RTM):
  →  { type: send_message, channel, text, thread_ts? }
  ←  { type: message, ... }
  ←  { type: presence_change, user, presence }

REST:
  GET /channels/{ws_id}                  → list
  GET /history/{channel_id}?cursor       → messages
  POST /upload                           → file_id
  GET /search?q=...&workspace=...        → results
```

**Observability**

- `message_send_p99_ms` (client → ack) — target < 200 ms in-region.
- `message_delivery_p99_ms` (post → other-client receive) — target < 500 ms same-workspace.
- `ws_reconnect_storm_rate` per pool — paged when reconnects/sec > 10× baseline.
- `cassandra_write_p99_ms` per workspace — target < 50 ms.
- `search_index_lag_seconds` per workspace — target < 10 s.
- `slack_connect_hop_p99_ms` — target < 1 s for cross-shard reactions.
- `notif_dispatch_p99_ms` from persist event — target < 5 s for mentions.
- SLO: 99.99% message persistence (no lost messages); 99.9% real-time delivery within 1 s for in-region same-workspace.

**Multi-region and DR**

- **Replication mode:** workspace pinned to a primary shard in one region; Cassandra cross-region async replication for DR (read replicas + log shipping). EU-region workspaces stay in EU for compliance/data-residency. Slack Connect bridges hop cross-region only when a shared channel's home shard is in another region.
- **RTO:** ~5 min for an MS Server pool failover (reconnect with cursor); ~15 min for a workspace's primary-shard region failover (promote replica + redirect MS Server pool).
- **RPO:** zero on persist (Cassandra `LOCAL_QUORUM` + idempotent retries); ~1 min on cross-region replication for DR.
- **Failover cadence:** quarterly DR exercises per region; weekly drain-mode deploy chaos.
- **Cross-region cost:** moderate — Slack Connect bridges and DR replication. Most traffic stays single-region per workspace.

### 33. Design Zoom (Video Conferencing)
#### Problem
Multi-party real-time video/audio calls with screen share, recording, and chat — at scale.
#### Core
TODO

Write the whole answer as you would give it in sixty seconds, 200 to 300 words, standing alone.
#### Summary
**The picture in your head:** a telephone switchboard from the early 20th century, but for video. In a direct peer-to-peer call with 8 people, every person needs a separate cable to every other person — that is 56 cables total, and your home internet has to send 7 separate video streams. Instead, Zoom inserts a relay box in the middle (the SFU). You send your video once to the relay box, and it decides which quality version to forward to each of the other 7 participants. You still send one stream; the relay does all the distribution.

**The approaches people actually take:**
TODO. Two or three things a competent engineer might reach for, in plain language and before any product name, with what each one buys and roughly when it wins.

**The single-request walkthrough:** you join a 5-person Zoom call. Your client does two things in parallel: it opens a WebSocket connection to Zoom's signaling server (this is the control channel — mute, raise hand, who joined/left), and it establishes a WebRTC connection over UDP to the nearest SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit — the relay box). Your camera is encoding three simultaneous video streams at 180p/200kbps, 480p/800kbps, and 720p/1.5Mbps — this is called simulcast (the camera produces three quality levels at once, each a separate UDP stream). The SFU receives all three. For each of the other 4 participants, the SFU independently decides which layer to forward: the person speaking gets the 720p layer sent to their tile, participants showing as thumbnails get 180p, and anyone on a congested wifi connection gets whatever fits their available bandwidth. The SFU makes this decision continuously using TWCC (Transport-Wide Congestion Control) — per-packet feedback from each receiver that tells the SFU how much packet loss and delay that person is seeing. When your wifi degrades mid-call, the SFU receives a TWCC report saying "I'm losing 15% of packets" and switches you to the 180p layer — quality dips, but the call does not drop.

**The pieces (and what each one is for):**
- **Signaling server (WebSocket)** — handles control messages: joining, muting, raising hand, participant list updates. Relatively low bandwidth and tolerant of 200ms latency. Kept completely separate from media because even a tiny delay in video is visible but a 200ms delay on a mute event is invisible.
- **SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit)** — the relay box. Receives one video upload from each participant and forwards the right layer to each receiver. Critically, the SFU does NOT decode or re-encode video — it just selects which of the pre-encoded simulcast layers to forward. This makes it cheap: one SFU server can relay a 50-person meeting using maybe 10% of a CPU core for video, versus an MCU (see below) which would need full transcoding power.
- **MCU (Multipoint Control Unit)** — a heavier alternative to the SFU. The MCU decodes all video inputs, composites them into a single "gallery view" frame, re-encodes it, and sends each participant one stream. Used for webinars (1 presenter, thousands of view-only attendees) because each viewer pays for only one downlink stream instead of N. Cost: CPU scales with number of active speakers; adds ~30-80ms transcode latency.
- **TWCC (Transport-Wide Congestion Control)** — a feedback mechanism where the receiver reports to the sender: "I received packet 1042 fine, 1043 was late, 1044-1047 I never got." The sender uses this to estimate available bandwidth and the SFU uses it to switch simulcast layers per-receiver. This is the loop that makes quality degrade gracefully instead of the call freezing.
- **FEC (Forward Error Correction)** — the sender adds redundant packets so that if a small number of UDP packets are lost in transit, the receiver can reconstruct the missing data without asking for a retransmit. Audio gets stronger FEC than video because a 200ms audio glitch is far more noticeable than a momentary video artifact.
- **Cascade SFUs** — for cross-region meetings (half the participants in EU, half in US), each group connects to a regional SFU and the two SFUs forward streams to each other over Zoom's backbone. Each participant pays only a local network hop to their nearest SFU; the SFU-to-SFU backbone link is optimized separately.

**The thing that makes it hard:** imagine a 1000-person Zoom webinar. In SFU mode, each viewer's device would need to decode and composite ~1000 video streams — that melts any laptop or phone. But just switching to MCU for all meetings is also wrong: MCU requires the server to decode and re-encode all video, which costs enormous CPU and adds transcode latency. The hard part is choosing the right mode per meeting. The solution: use SFU for normal meetings (up to ~50 active participants) with "active speaker selection" — only the top K speakers get high-resolution layers forwarded to each receiver; everyone else is paused or sent a thumbnail. Switch to MCU only for webinars where viewers don't publish video at all.

**Why this design and what it costs:** SFU + simulcast is the default because the sender pays a 1.5x upload cost (three quality layers instead of one) in exchange for the SFU never needing to transcode. At 10 million concurrent meetings, avoiding transcoding on the SFU saves colossal amounts of CPU. The tradeoff you accept is that senders with very constrained upload bandwidth pay slightly more, but that's almost always the right trade at scale.

**If you were building it tomorrow:**
- WebRTC stack on client (libwebrtc), regional SFU clusters (Jitsi Videobridge or custom), signaling via WebSocket.
- Each SFU handles ~200 concurrent meetings on a 16-core machine (no transcode, mostly forwarding).
- Core SFU forwarding loop pseudocode:
  ```
  on packet_received(sender, rtp_packet):
    layer = detect_simulcast_layer(rtp_packet)
    for each receiver in meeting:
      target_layer = select_layer(receiver.twcc_bandwidth, receiver.ui_layout)
      if layer == target_layer:
        forward(receiver, rtp_packet)
  ```
- On TWCC report showing >5% loss: downgrade that receiver's target layer. On recovery: upgrade. On persistent loss: switch to audio-only for that receiver.

#### Clarifying questions and how each answer forks the design
- Max participants per call?
- Recording and storage?
- E2E encryption?
- Webinars (1-to-many, thousands of viewers)?
- Geographic distribution?

**How the answers shape the design**

| If the answer is… | Then the design… |
|---|---|
| Small calls (a few participants) | mesh or SFU is optional; an SFU (selective forwarding unit) scales better past a handful |
| Large calls | an SFU that forwards each sender's stream to others, avoiding N-squared encoding |
| Webinars (thousands of viewers) | switch the broadcast leg to HLS/CDN distribution, not per-viewer SFU streams |
| Recording | a server-side recording pipeline compositing streams to object storage |
| E2E encryption | keys stay on clients, which rules out server-side recording and transcoding of media |
| Geographic distribution | place media servers near participants and relay between regions to cut latency |
#### Requirements and scale, derived out loud
**Requirements**

- **FR:** create meeting, join, video/audio per participant, screen share, chat, record
- **NFR:** <150ms one-way latency, support 1k participants/meeting, scale to millions of concurrent meetings

**Scale**

- **DAU / concurrent:** ~300M daily participants (Zoom pandemic-peak public); ~10M concurrent meetings at peak (assumes ~5% of DAU in a meeting at any moment during business overlap, 300M × 5%/avg-5-per-meeting ≈ 3M; 10M is conservative/ceiling)
- **Per-meeting size / bitrate:** avg ~5 participants/meeting (Zoom-disclosed); 720p ≈ ~1.5 Mbps top simulcast layer; aggregate "tens of Tbps" arises from 10M × 5 × ~3 Mbps full-duplex (see below)
- **Media stream bitrate:** 180p ≈ 200 kbps, 480p ≈ 800 kbps, 720p ≈ 1.5 Mbps, 1080p ≈ 3 Mbps + audio Opus ≈ 40–50 kbps; simulcast publishes 180p + 480p + 720p simultaneously → 200 + 800 + 1500 ≈ ~2.5 Mbps upload total
- **Per-meeting SFU bandwidth:** 5-person meeting → uploads = 5 × 2.5 Mbps = 12.5 Mbps in; downlinks per receiver ≈ 4 streams × ~1 Mbps adaptive (active speaker ~1.5 Mbps + 3 thumbnails ~0.2 Mbps + audio) ≈ ~4 Mbps × 5 receivers ≈ ~20 Mbps out
- **Aggregate SFU traffic:** 10M meetings × 5 participants × ~3 Mbps avg full-duplex (ingress + egress mixed) = 10M × 5 × 3 Mbps = ~150 Tbps; distributed across regional SFU clusters → ~10–30 Tbps per major region
- **Recording storage:** assume 30% of meetings recorded; avg duration 30 min × 60 s × ~1.5 Mbps composited / 8 = ~340 MB/recording; 50M meetings/day × 30% = ~15M recordings (ceiling); paid-tier subset ≈ ~3M recordings/day actually stored × 340 MB ≈ ~1 PB/day; 90-day default retention → 1 PB × 90 = ~90 PB hot tier
- **Signaling load:** 10M concurrent meetings × ~5 participants = 50M concurrent WebSocket connections; ~10 control events/min/participant (mute, video toggle, presence) → 50M × 10 / 60 ≈ ~8M events/s on control plane
- **Meeting metadata:** ~5 KB per meeting = (participants list + timing + recording ref + chat refs + scheduling); 50M meetings/day × 5 KB = ~250 GB/day into wide-column store

**Raw material, from the old Common Mistakes:**

- *Naive SFU sends one quality to everyone.* Either you transcode (expensive) or you punish the slow receivers / starve the fast ones; simulcast is the mechanism — sender publishes 3 bitrates, SFU picks per-receiver.
- *TCP for media.* Head-of-line blocking on retransmits destroys real-time UX; UDP with FEC + selective retransmit is the only viable transport.
- *MCU as default.* MCU costs CPU linear in inputs and a transcode hop of latency; reserve for webinars and very-low-end clients.
- *Mixing signaling and media on one connection.* Signaling is stateful and tolerable to 200 ms RTT; media is real-time; different transports, different planes.
- *No active-speaker selection in large meetings.* Each receiver pulls N streams; client decode melts at scale. Top-K speakers high-res, others paused/thumbnail.
- *E2E mode without acknowledging the trade-offs.* E2E breaks cloud recording, transcription, telephony bridge — explicit product trade.

**How to read the diagram:** signaling helps clients discover and join the meeting, but the real weight sits in the media path. Clients send audio and video to media relays, which decide what to forward to whom and at what quality.

**Why the flow is shaped this way:** direct peer-to-peer meshes fall apart quickly as participant count rises. Centralized relays let the system adapt bandwidth and quality in a controlled way instead of asking every client to send everything to everyone.

**What this layout buys you:** more stable calls and better scalability for group meetings. The tradeoff is that media relays become performance-critical infrastructure with strict latency requirements.
#### Deep dive
**must-say**

**SFU vs MCU vs P2P:**

| Mode | Server cost | Bandwidth (participant) | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P2P** (mesh) | none | uploads × (N-1) | 1:1, very small (≤4) |
| **SFU** | low (no transcode) | 1 up, (N-1) down | small-to-medium meetings |
| **MCU** (mixer) | high (CPU) | 1 up, 1 down | webinars, low-end clients |

Zoom mostly SFU; switch to MCU for webinars.

**Simulcast.** Each sender publishes three video streams simultaneously — 180p, 480p, 720p — at roughly 200 kbps, 800 kbps, and 1.5 Mbps. The SFU picks which one to forward to each receiver based on receiver context: who's the active speaker (gets 720p), who's a thumbnail (gets 180p), who's on a slow network (gets whatever fits). Without simulcast, the SFU would either need to transcode (expensive) or pick one quality for everyone (bad UX in heterogeneous networks). Sender pays ~1.5× upload bandwidth — well worth it.

**Adaptive bitrate (sender side).** TWCC (Transport-Wide Congestion Control) sends per-packet feedback from receiver back to sender — packet loss, RTT, observed bandwidth. The sender's encoder adjusts target bitrate in real time, drops a simulcast layer if upload is congested, and degrades resolution gracefully. This is the loop that handles "wifi got worse mid-meeting" without anyone explicitly noticing — quality dips, then recovers when the network improves.

**Recording.** Cloud recording = SFU forwards every participant's stream into a dedicated recorder process, which behaves like an MCU: decode each input, composite into a grid layout, encode to MP4, upload to object store in chunks. Recorder is stateful with checkpointed buffers — crash-restart resumes from the last checkpoint rather than losing the meeting. Client-side recording is the fallback for E2E-encrypted meetings where the server can't see unencrypted media; each client records locally and uploads after.

**E2E encryption (opt-in mode).** Default mode encrypts media on the wire (DTLS-SRTP) but the SFU holds the keys — required because the SFU forwards streams and cloud features (recording, transcription, telephony bridge) need server-side plaintext. *Opt-in E2E mode* uses per-meeting keys negotiated client-to-client (current generation uses a public-key handshake rooted in each user's device key), and the SFU forwards opaque ciphertext without ever holding keys. The trade-off is sharp: cloud recording, live transcription, dial-in via PSTN, and browser-only join all break in E2E mode (they depend on server-side decryption). E2E is therefore reserved for sensitive meetings where those features can be sacrificed; the recording fallback is client-side capture by an authorised participant.

**Network selection.** Anycast routing + latency probing picks the closest SFU at session start. For mixed-region meetings, cascade SFUs: each region's participants connect locally, and the regional SFUs forward streams to each other over the backbone. Cascading adds one hop of latency (~30-50ms transatlantic) but keeps each participant's first-mile short and avoids forcing everyone onto a single distant SFU. The cascade primary is picked by median-participant-latency heuristic — minimise total perceived latency, accept that one outlier (the lone EU person in a US meeting) eats extra latency rather than punishing the majority.

**Simulcast layer selection per receiver.**

The SFU never transcodes — it just picks a layer per receiver and forwards. Selection inputs are receiver bandwidth (TWCC per-packet feedback gives observed loss / RTT / available bitrate) and viewport context (active speaker gets the high layer; thumbnails get the lowest; pinned tiles override). Sender pays ~1.5× upload to publish all three layers; the SFU recoups that cost dozens of times over because it never has to decode + re-encode. *[Source: webrtchacks SFU cascading, WebRTC Octo protocol]*

**MCU mixer mechanics for webinars.** Above ~50 participants the SFU's per-receiver downlink math (each receiver pulls ~N video streams) breaks even powerful clients — decode + composite client-side melts low-end devices and saturates downlink. MCU mode flips it: server decodes all inputs, composites them into one grid frame (active speaker large, others small), re-encodes once, and sends a *single* stream to every viewer. Per-viewer downlink becomes constant (one stream regardless of meeting size). Cost: a transcode hop of latency (+30-80ms) and CPU linear in active streams. Webinars (1→thousands view-only) live entirely in MCU mode because viewers don't publish video at all; for hybrid (panel + audience), the panel publishes via SFU and the MCU composites only the panel for the audience. *[Source: WebRTC SFU vs MCU literature]*

**Cascade SFU forwarding (Octo-style).** Multi-region meetings connect each participant to a local SFU; SFUs then forward streams between themselves over Zoom's backbone. The forwarding header (similar to Jitsi's Octo: a fixed-length wrapper over RTP) lets bridges tag streams without breaking SRTP encryption end-to-end at the SFU layer. Hop-by-hop NACK retransmission means a packet lost between Participant A and SFU-1 is recovered locally — SFU-2 never sees the loss — so jitter buffers can be smaller and end-to-end latency stays sane despite the extra hop. Bridges typically run a full mesh; for very large meetings, a tree topology routes through a primary cascade root. *[Source: webrtchacks SFU cascading]*
#### Where it breaks
**must-say**

**Bottlenecks**

- **Huge meeting** (1000 participants) — pure SFU breaks because each receiver needs N−1 downlink streams; decode + composite client-side melts low-end devices. Switch to MCU mode (server composites to one stream per receiver) or aggressive active-speaker selection (top-K speakers at high res, everyone else paused or thumbnail).
- **Network congestion** (bad wifi mid-meeting) — TWCC detects loss and the sender drops to a lower simulcast layer; if even that's unsustainable, fall back to audio-only (audio is ~50 kbps and gets stronger FEC). Quality dips visibly but the call doesn't drop.
- **Packet loss** (UDP drops 5-20%) — FEC (forward error correction) recovers small loss without retransmit; selective retransmit handles larger loss for keyframes; jitter buffer absorbs reordering. All three run in milliseconds at the player.
- **DDoS on signaling** (Zoombomb attempts: thousands of join attempts on one meeting ID) — rate-limit join attempts per IP and per meeting ID at the signaling endpoint; meeting JWT is short-lived and bound to invitee email; CAPTCHA on suspicious patterns; waiting room enforces host approval before media plane setup.
- **Cross-region quality** (half EU, half US) — cascade SFUs minimise the hops by connecting each participant locally; without cascading, half the meeting eats transatlantic latency. The SFU-to-SFU link is over Zoom's backbone, optimised for this case.
- **Simulcast upload cost** (sender publishes 3 layers simultaneously, ~2.5 Mbps total instead of 1.5 Mbps for the top layer) — sender pays ~1.5× upload bandwidth. Mitigation is acceptance: the alternative is server-side transcoding, which is dramatically more expensive at SFU scale, or single-bitrate forwarding which gives bad UX in heterogeneous networks. Simulcast wins on operational economics. SVC (scalable video coding) is a future direction that gets the same flexibility from one bitstream but ecosystem support lags simulcast.
- **Cascade SFU NACK domain** — a packet lost between two SFUs over backbone needs hop-by-hop retransmission; if backbone link flaps, the cascade root SFU sees a flood of NACKs from downstream bridges. Mitigation is per-hop retransmit budgets and FEC pre-applied on the cascade link so transient backbone loss doesn't cascade into full retransmits.
- **Recorder crash mid-meeting** — cloud recording = an MCU-style process holding decoded frame buffers; a crash without checkpoints loses the meeting. Recorder is a stateful service with checkpointed buffers (every 5-10s) flushed to object store as chunks; crash-restart replays the SFU stream from the last checkpoint and resumes encoding to the same chunked output.

**Failure modes**

| Layer | Failure | Detection | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| SFU | Pod crash mid-meeting | Heartbeat loss + signaling-side liveness | Reconnect to backup SFU in same cluster; clients re-publish; brief blip while ABR settles |
| Media path | Persistent UDP packet loss > 20% | Per-receiver loss telemetry | FEC + selective retransmit; degrade to lower simulcast layer; fall back to audio-only |
| Signaling | WebSocket disconnect during meeting | Per-session WS health probe | Reconnect with session token; meeting state preserved server-side |
| Cascade backbone | SFU-to-SFU link flap on transatlantic peering | NACK rate spike on bridge | Per-hop retransmit budgets; FEC pre-applied on cascade link; reroute via different bridge |
| MCU mixer | Server CPU saturation under N video inputs | Encode latency p99 | Reduce active-speaker count; pause inactive participants; horizontally scale mixer fleet |
| License/JWT | Meeting JWT validation failure under join storm | Auth 5xx rate | Short-lived tokens cached at signaling edge; rate-limit per IP; CAPTCHA on suspicious patterns |
| Recorder | Crash during long meeting | Recorder process liveness | Checkpointed buffers every 5-10s flushed to object store; restart replays from last checkpoint |
| Region | SFU cluster regional outage | Per-region SFU health | Anycast routing reroutes to nearest healthy cluster; ongoing meetings degrade or migrate via cascade |

**Unresolved**

3. Why UDP for media instead of TCP/QUIC?
4. How do you handle a "Zoombombing" attack (uninvited joiners)?
5. How does cross-region work — half the participants in EU, half in US?
6. How do you record a meeting reliably without dropping content?

#### Answers to drill questions
1. Almost never for normal meetings. SFU + simulcast + active-speaker selection (top-K speakers at high res, thumbnails or paused for the rest) scales into the hundreds. Pure MCU is reserved for webinars (1→thousands view-only) and low-end clients that can't decode many streams. *If pushed:* real limit isn't participant count but per-receiver downlink and decode budget; SFU drops inactive participants to low-res or pauses them before switching to MCU. MCU costs a transcode hop of latency and CPU linear in active streams — last resort.

2. FEC (forward error correction) recovers most loss without retransmit; jitter buffer absorbs reordering. Sender drops to lower simulcast layer via TWCC. *If pushed:* persistent loss → degrade to audio-only (audio gets stronger FEC + redundancy); if even audio fails, signaling stays alive over WebSocket so user can rejoin without losing session state.

3. TCP retransmits stall the entire stream waiting for a lost packet — fatal for real-time. UDP lets you drop and continue; FEC/retransmit selectively at app layer. *If pushed:* QUIC has unordered streams which would work, but WebRTC predates production QUIC and ecosystems standardized on RTP-over-UDP; ICE/STUN/TURN solves NAT traversal which TCP can't easily do.

4. Waiting rooms by default; meeting passwords; per-meeting random IDs (no enumeration). Host can lock meeting after start. *If pushed:* signaling endpoint rate-limits join attempts per IP and per meeting ID; CAPTCHA on suspicious patterns; meeting JWT short-lived and bound to invitee email; ML-detect screen-share abuse post-join.

5. Each participant connects to their nearest SFU; SFUs cascade (SFU-to-SFU forward). Adds one hop of latency but keeps each participant's first-mile cheap. *If pushed:* Zoom uses median-participant-latency heuristic to pick the cascade primary; for unbalanced groups (one outlier), the outlier eats extra latency rather than punishing the majority.

6. Cloud recording = SFU pulls all streams into a dedicated MCU-style recorder process which encodes to MP4 and uploads to S3 in chunks. *If pushed:* recorder is a separate stateful service with checkpointed buffers — crash-restart resumes from last checkpoint. Client-side recording is the fallback for local-only / E2E-encrypted meetings where the server can't see unencrypted media.
